In the present system of appointments, the judiciary initiates the proposals to 
appoint the Judges in the High Courts and Supreme Courts and the onus of 
addressing the issue rests with the Judiciary. However, the Government is committed 
to social diversity in the appointment of Judges in the Higher Judiciary. The Hon'ble 
Minister of Law & Justice has been requesting the Chief Justices of High Court s that 
while sending proposals for appointment of Judges, due consideration be given to 
suitable candidates belonging to Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, Other 
Backward Classes, Minorities and Women to ensure social diversity in appointment 
of Judges in High Courts.  
 
Further observation of the Committee: 
3.8  The Committee observes that the views/ comments on draft Memoranda of 
Procedure (MoP)  of the Supreme Court are still awaited . Whenever it is 
finalized, the Government may factor in the aspect of social diversity into it.  The 
Committee desires that the Ministry may pursue the Supreme Court to send its 
views on the MoP at the earliest. 
3.9 The Committee also notes that the class/category-wise data in respect of 
the judges who are presently serving in the Supreme Court and High Courts is 
available from the year 2017. For the remaining judges who are presently 
serving in the Supreme Court and High Courts, data has been sought from the 
judiciary by the Ministry .  This process may be expedited with judiciary and it 
may be forwarded to th e Committee for examination as and when such an 
exercise is completed.  
 
 
 
 

 21 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
EXPLORING THE POSSIBILITIES OF INCREASING THE RETIREMENT 
AGE OF HIGH COURT AND SUPREME COURT JUDGES 
 
3.10 Many stakeholders had also raised objections to the post -retirement 
assignments given to judges, and the Committee is accordingly, of the view that 
with the increase in the age of retirement of judges, the practice of post -
retirement assignments to judges of Supreme Court and High Courts in 
bodies/institutions financed from public exchequer may be reassessed to ensure 
their impartiality.                 (Para 49) 
 
Action Taken 
3.11 Appointments of retired Supreme Court Judges to various Constitutional posts , 
Commissions, Tribunals etc. are made by different Ministries/Departments as per 
relevant rules laid down by the respective appointing authority. Some of these bodies 
require expertise and experience possessed by the Judges of the Supreme Court /High 
Courts. 
 
Further observation of the Committee: 
3.12 Though t he Committee takes cognizance of the stand of the Committee 
regarding appointments of retired Supreme Court Judges to various 
Constitutional posts, Commissions, Tribunals etc. made by different 
Ministries/Departments as per relevant rules laid down by the respective 
appointing authority,  nevertheless the Committee suggests that the entire 
gamut of issues related to such appointments of retired judges may be 
comprehensively studied again and relooked upon by the Ministry.   
 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
VACATIONS IN THE SUPREME COURT AND HIGH COURTS 
3.13 During the deliberations on this issue, most of the members were of the 
opinion that the need of the hour is an efficient judiciary that is not only 
committed to meeting the needs and interests of the citizens but also 
communicates this commitment by modif ying its practices to suit the needs of 

 22 
the country. The judiciary, therefore, needs to be sensitized from shutting down 
courts en masse for a couple of months a year.             (Para 61) 
  
3.14    The demand for doing away with vacations in the Courts emanates 
primarily due to two factors, one is the huge pendency of cases in our courts, 
and the other is the inconvenience faced by the litigants during the vacations of 
the courts. A common man holds a perception that despite having such huge 
pendency of cases their judges go on long vacations. Further during the 
vacations, the litigants have to suffer a lot despite having a handful of vacation 
courts/benches.                 (Para 66) 
  
3.15    Though in this connection it may be noted that for the past few years, the 
pendency in the Supreme Court has remained static and in the year 2022 the 
disposal of cases was more than the number of cases instituted in that year. Thus 
it can be seen that as f ar as the disposal of cases is concerned, the performance 
of our Supreme Court is quite good. The problem lies with the legacy arrears of 
about 35000.                 (Para 67) 
  
3.16    From the foregoing discussion it can be seen that vacations in the 
Judiciary are not the only factor for pendency. For reducing pendency there is a 
need to have a multipronged strategy. However, at the same time, it is an 
undeniable fact that vacations in the judiciary are a 'colonial legacy' and with 
entire court going on vacation en masse  causes deep inconvenience to the 
litigants.                   (Para 70) 
  
3.17.    In this scenario, the Committee is of the view that the suggestion of the 
former Chief Justice of India Shri RM Lodha on court vacations, that instead of 
all the judges going on vacation, all at one time, individual judges should take 
their leave at different times through the year so that the courts are constantly 
open and there are always benches present to hear cases, should be considered 
by the Judiciary.                  (Para 71) 
  
Action taken on para Nos. 3.13 to  3. 17:  
  
As a part of the recommendations of the 133 rd Report, the Parliamentary 
Standing Committee has endorsed the suggestion of former Chief Justice of India 
Shri R.M. Lodha on Court vacations, who opined that instead of all the judges going 
on vacations, all at one time, individual judges should take their leave at different 

 23 
times through the year, so that the courts are constantly open and are always present 
to hear cases, which should be considered by Judiciary. Since the vacations for the 
Supreme Court and various High Courts are prescribed as per the rules framed by the 
respective courts for which they have been empowered under the provisions of the 
Constitution, the reco mmendations of the Hon‟ble Committee has been sent by the 
Department of Justice to the Supreme Court of India  and the Registrar Generals of 
the State High Courts after due approval of the Hon‟ble MoS (I/C), Law & 
Justice.  Their response is awaited.  
 
Further observation of the Committee 
3.18 The Department may take up the issue with  the Supreme Court of 
India and the Registrar Generals of the State High Courts  to forward their 
response on the recommendations of the Committee regarding staggered 
vacation by individual judges at different times of the year, at the earliest , so 
that the issue of vacation can be settled for once and all. Once this issue is 
finalized, the Courts will have more days at its disposal, which will enable it to 
reduce the pendency  and mitigate the inconvenience presently being faced by 
the litigants, to a large extent.   
 
 
 
*** 
  

 24 
CHAPTER IV 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF 
WHICH FINAL REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT HAVE NOT 
BEEN RECEIVED:  
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
MANDATORY DECLARATION OF ASSETS BY THE JUDGES OF THE 
SUPREME COURT AND HIGH COURTS 
  
4.1   As a general practice, all constitutional functionaries and government 
servants must file annual returns of their assets and liabilities. The Supreme 
Court has gone to the ex tent of holding that the public has a right to know the 
assets of those standing for elections as MPs or MLAs. When so, it belies logic 
that Judges don't need to disclose their assets and liabilities. Anybody holding 
public office and drawing a salary from  the exchequer should mandatorily 
furnish annual returns of their property. (Para 79 of the report) 
  
4.2    Declaration of assets by the Judges of the Higher Judiciary will only bring 
more trust and credibility into the system. As the last resolution of t he Supreme 
Court on the declaration of assets by Judges on a voluntary basis is not complied 
with, the Committee recommends the Government to bring about appropriate 
legislation to make it mandatory for Judges of the higher judiciary (Supreme 
Court and High Courts) to furnish their property returns on an annual basis to 
the appropriate authority. (Para 82 of the report) 
  
Action taken on para No.4.0 and 4.1: 
  
4.3 Based on the recommendations made by the Parliamentary Standing 
Committee, this Department is proposing to frame Rules under the High Court 
Judges Act, 1954 and Supreme Court Judges Act, 1958 to lay down a procedure for 
making statutory provisions in the Rules for  Declaration of Assets by the Judges of 
the Supreme Court and High Court Judges  on their initial appointment and thereafter 
every year by the due date.   Consultation with the Registry of the Supreme Court has 
since been initiated, soliciting their views in the matter.   Their response, however, is 
awaited. 

 25 
 
Further observation of the Committee: 
4.4 The Department may fastrack the consultation process with the Registry 
of the Supreme Court for making statutory provisions in the Rules 
for Declaration of Assets by the Judges of the Supreme Court and High Court 
Judges on their initial appointment and apprise the Committee of the same.

 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee 
on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice, having been authorized by the 
Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this One Hundred 
and Forty Fifth Report on Demands for Grants (2025-26) pertaining to the 
Department of Personnel and Training. 
2. In accordance with the constitutional requirement under Article 113, the 
estimated expenditure of Ministries/Departments of Government of India projected 
under various Demands for Grants for the upcoming financial year needs to be voted 
by Parliament. As a sequel thereto, Demands for Grants of the relevant 
Ministries/Departments stand referred to the concerned Department-related 
Parliamentary Standing Committee to make a close scrutiny thereof under Rule 270 of

performance, programmes, policies of the Department of Personnel and Training 
vis-à-vis expenditure made out of Consolidated Fund of India in the current financial 
year.

Wings of Department of Personnel and Training:  
1.4 Various wings of DoPT are as under: 
(i) Establishment Officer's (EO) Wing - The Establishment Officer's Wing 
deals with the matters relating to senior appointments under the 
Government of India requiring approval of the Appointments 
Committee of the Cabinet (ACC). 
(ii) Services & Vigilance (S&V) Wing - The Services & Vigilance Wing 
handles matters relating to administration of Rules on all the service 
matters in respect of All India Services and acts as the nodal agency in 
the arena of vigilance and anti-corruption.  
(iii) Personnel Policy Wing - The Personnel Policy Wing is responsible for 
framing and revising rules and regulations regarding service conditions 
of the employees and personnel policies of the Central Government 
employees other than All India Service Officers. This wing handles the 
work related to Service conditions of Central Government, Reservation 
Policy of the Government, Joint Consultative Machinery (JCM) and 
Cadre Review. This wing also looks after the work related to the 
allocation of State cadre employees consequent upon the 
reorganization of the States and redeployment and retraining of surplus 
Staff of various Central Government Organisations.  
(iv) AT, IR, Welfare Wing - The AT, IR, Welfare Wing is responsible for 
governing and implementation of the RTI Act. Also handles the 
administrative matters relating to the Administrative Tribunals and 
Central Information Commission. This wing also handles the work 
related to internal Administration and Coordination of DoPT and 
welfare activities for benefit of the employees of the Government.  
(v) Training Wing – The Training Wing acts as the nodal agency for 
capacity building of Government functionaries and is primarily 
responsible for formulating policies regarding training.  
(vi) The Central Secretariat Wing - The Central Secretariat Wing deals 
with the matters related to Cadre Management of the Central 
Secretariat Service, Central Secretariat Stenographers’ Service and the 
Central Secretariat Clerical Service.

Major responsibilities/functions of the Department of Personnel and Training: 
1.6 The following are major responsibilities/functions of DoPT: 
Personnel Policies  
1.7 The Department is responsible for framing rules and regulations governing 
service conditions including recruitment rules, promotions and seniority, Flexible 
Complementing Scheme, Leave Travel Concession, Deputation and Leave of 
employees. Personnel are recruited for the Central Government by the Union Public 
Service Commission through competitive examinations conducted by them for 
appointments to higher civil services and through the Staff Selection Commission for 
non-gazetted staff in Group ‘B’ & ‘C’ categories. 
 Reservation  
1.8  In order to achieve the objective of upliftment and welfare of the Scheduled 
Castes and Scheduled Tribes, Other Backward Classes and Persons with Disabilities 
and Economically Weaker Sections (EWS); the Department frames policies to 
provide reservation to these groups in various Central Government services and for 
monitoring its implementation.  
Cadre Management  
1.9  This Department is responsible for the management of the cadres of All India 
Services (AIS) (IAS, IPS, and IFoS) and all three Secretariat Services namely Central 
Secretariat Services (CSS), Central Secretariat Stenographers’ Services (CSSS) and 
Central Secretariat Clerical Services (CSCS). In addition, this Department frames and 
revises Rules and Regulations regarding conditions of the All India Services, such as 
Indian Police Service (IPS) and Indian Forest Service (IFoS), in consultation with the 
Ministry of Home Affairs and Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change 
respectively. 
Senior Appointments under the Government of India  
1.10  The Department deals with appointments at senior level and personnel 
policies of the Government of India. All proposals for senior appointments under the 
Government of India, which require the approval of the Appointments Committee of 
the Cabinet (ACC), are processed by the Department. These include board-level 
appointments to Central Public Sector Undertakings and appointments under the 
Central Staffing Scheme for posts of Joint Secretary, Director, and Deputy Secretary 

 
17 
in Ministries /Departments. In addition, all appointments by promotion, which require 
the approval of the ACC, are also processed by the Department.  
Training Policy and Programmes  
1.11  The Department is the nodal authority to impart training to the government 
functionaries. The Training Wing of the Department formulates policies and 
implements its training programmes by identifying areas of training, designing 
training programmes, development of trainers and training capabilities and 
administering policies in training. Major training activities undertaken during the year 
are (i) In-service training of AIS/CSS/CSSS officers (ii) Mid-Career Training of IAS 
Officers (iii) Post Graduate Programmes in Public Policy/Sustainable 
Development/Management (iv) State Category Training Programme (SCTP); (v) 
Trainer Development Programme (TDP); (vi) Comprehensive Online Modified 
Modules for Induction Training (COMMIT); (vii) Augmentation of the Capacity of 
Training Institutions (ACTI); (viii) Integrated Government Online Training 
Programme (i-GOT); and (ix) National Programme for Civil Services Capacity 
Building (NPCSCB)– Mission Karmayogi.  Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of 
Administration (LBSNAA), Mussourie, Uttarakhand and Institute of Secretariat 
Training and Management (ISTM), New Delhi are two premier training institutions, 
attached to this Department.  
Mission Karmayogi & e-HRMS  
1.12 National Programme for Civil Services Capacity Building (NPCSCB) – 
Mission Karmayogi is being implemented with the goal of systematically imparting 
behavioral and functional competencies needed by a government official to best 
discharge their assigned roles and aims to effect a signal shift in competency driven 
training and Human Resource (HR) management of officials, by transitioning from a 
‘rule-based’ system to a ‘role-based’ system of capacity building.  
1.13  Through the adoption of modern technological tools such as a digital platform 
- the integrated Government online Training (i-GoT) portal - 
https://igotkarmayogi.gov.in/ and with effective harnessing of artificial Intelligence, 
machine learning and data analytics, Mission Karmayogi endeavors to break silos in 
capacity development and democratize knowledge on an equitable basis across civil 
services, by bringing easy access to world class continuous learning opportunities for 
all government officials. The NPCSCB facilitates data-driven decisions for training 
and personnel management through the electronic Human Resources Management 
System (e-HRMS), which has now been revamped as e-HRMS2.0 and also integrated 
with the i-GOT portal.  

 
18 
Administrative Vigilance Division 
1.14  The Department is the nodal agency responsible for the formulation and 
implementation of vigilance and anti-corruption policies of the Government. 
Administrative Vigilance Wing in the Department oversees government programme 
for maintenance of discipline and eradication of corruption from public service. The 
Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) advises the Central Government on all 
vigilance matters. The jurisdiction of the Commission extends to all the organisations 
to which the executive powers of the Union of India extend. To deal with 
international cooperation on these aspects an International Cooperation Cell was 
created in this Department.   
Joint Consultative Machinery 
1.15 The Government provides for a Joint Consultative Machinery for joint 
consultation at three levels between the Central Government and its employees for 
promoting harmonious relations and securing the optimum level of co-operation 
between the Central Government and its employees in matters of common concern. 
The objective is to increase the efficiency of public services along with the well-being 
of the employees. The three tiers are:  
(a)  National Council – at the apex level, functioning under the Department of 
Personnel and Training.  
(b) Department Councils – functioning at the level of the Ministries / 
Departments.  
(c) Office Councils – functioning at offices/organisations under various Ministries 
/ Departments.  
Administrative Tribunal  
1.16  In order to provide speedy and inexpensive justice delivery system to the 
employees who feel aggrieved by Government decisions, the Government set up the 
Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) in 1985, which now deals with all cases 
relating to service matters. The CAT has 19 regular benches, 17 of which operate at 
the Principal seats of High Courts and the remaining two are at Jaipur and Lucknow. 
Staff Welfare  
1.17 The Central Government being the largest single employer in the country 
discharges its responsibility for looking after the welfare of employees through 
various welfare measures. The Department also extends support to various staff 
welfare measures. The DoPT is the nodal Department for registered societies set up 
for the welfare of the Government employees and their families. In addition, the 

 
19 
Department lays down policies for Departmental Canteens and supports the Resident 
Welfare Associations.  
Right to Information  
1.18 The Department has brought out a comprehensive law to ensure the right to 
information of the citizens of India in almost entire matters of governance at all levels 
from the Central Government to the local self-government. The Law (RTI Act, 2005) 
has provided a mechanism where the Central Information Commission, being the 
apex body at the Centre, facilitates its citizenry in accessing information in a time-
bound, hassle-free and affordable manner.

2.43 In response to a question regarding manpower and budgetary constraints, the 
Committee has been informed as under :- 
“IIPA has been getting Grant-in-aid to the tune of Rs.28.00 crores to Rs.32.00 
crores in the past years. However, the Grant-in-aid has been suddenly 
curtailed to its half i.e. Rs.15.00 crores for BE 2024-25. As such, IIPA has 
been facing huge resource crunch presently. The number of Training 
Programmes, Research Projects and other academic activities at IIPA have 
increased manifolds in recent years. The already existing infrastructure which 
is old and dilapidated needs renovation on urgent basis. Additional 
infrastructure like some additional rooms in Hostel for trainee officers and a 
new hostel is needed. Therefore, it is requested to provide some additional 
Grant-in-aid under R.E. 2024-25 to the tune of Rs.15.00 crores, over and 
above the sanctioned Grant of Rs.15.00 crores so that IIPA can function 
smoothly.” 
 2.44 The Committee recognizes the financial constraints faced by IIPA due to 
the substantial increase in training programs, research projects, and academic 
activities, along with the urgent need for infrastructure renovation and 
expansion. The current allocation seems to be insufficient, potentially impacting 
the quality and efficiency of IIPA’s operations. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends that an additional Grant-in-aid be provided, based on a 
comprehensive assessment of funding requirements, to support infrastructure 
improvements, meet growing academic demands, and sustain IIPA’s capacity to 
train officers effectively.

Civil Services Examination reforms 
4.3  To a specific question raised by the Committee on publishing of answer keys 
of Preliminary Examination of Civil Services to bring more transparency and reduce 
litigation, the Commission submitted as follows : 
“The Commission sought information from 14 different national level 
examination conducting bodies like State Public Service Commission, SSC, 
Banks, CBSE etc. (who are declaring provisional answer keys) regarding how 
the provisional/final answer keys before declaration of result of an 
examination has led to greater transparency and satisfaction to the candidates 
in terms of reduction in litigations/RTIs/Representations. 
 It is pertinent to mention that the process of declaration of provisional 
answer keys is a recent practice by various exam conducting bodies and the 
data available in this regard is also limited. Some of the exam conducting 
bodies, who have provided their inputs have given a generalized reply that the 
process of declaration of provisional answer key has led to greater 
satisfaction among the candidates. Some have stated that in case candidates 
are not satisfied with the answer key published by them, they opt to challenge 
it in Court, which delays the entire examination process. Based on the inputs 
received from 8 exam conducting bodies no clear view can be established 
regarding reduction / increase in litigation / representations.” 

 
49 
4.5   Due to the limited data available and mixed responses from eight exam bodies, 
no conclusive trend on litigation reduction or increase can be established. The practice 
of publishing provisional answer keys is relatively new, and its long-term effects 
remain uncertain. Further systematic analysis is needed to assess whether this measure 
significantly reduces representations, RTIs, and legal disputes. 
4.6  UPSC informed the Committee that it publishes the preliminary 
examination answer key only after completing the entire selection process. This 
delays candidates' ability to challenge potential errors before advancing to the 
next stage, undermining transparency and fairness. Such a practice can 
demoralize candidates and raise concerns about the validity of the examination. 
Despite rigorous scrutiny, the possibility of errors in the answer key cannot be 
entirely ruled out. To enhance credibility, fairness, and candidate confidence, the 
Committee reiterates its recommendation contained in para 4.5 of its 126th 
report that UPSC may explore and take steps to release the answer key 
immediately after the preliminary examination and provide candidates with an 
opportunity to raise objections before proceeding further.

4.7  The Committee had recommended in its previous Reports that an expert 
committee should be constituted to study the impact of the changes carried out in the 
scheme and syllabus of Civil Services Examination from time to time on

recommendations of expert committee i.e. Baswan Committee, the Department

Committee has submitted its report, which is currently under examination in the 
Department. 
4.9 The Committee notes the reply in this regard and welcomes the steps taken by 
the Department.  However, the Committee wishes to point out that delay in 
implementing necessary changes raises concerns about timely reforms in the 

 
50 
examination process. Given the importance of these recommendations in ensuring 
fairness and efficiency, swift action is needed to assess, finalize, and implement

Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) 
Human Resource Management 
6.1 A significant number of posts in CBI are filled on deputation from different 
organisations.  The Department has informed about the challenges in securing 
nominations from organizations for deputation of officials as under : 
 
i. “CBI is not receiving sufficient & suitable nominations of officers from State 
Police which has traditionally been a major source of induction, particularly 
in the rank of Inspector and below. 
ii. CBI is not receiving sufficient and suitable nominations because of shortage of 
manpower in the respective Lending Departments. 
iii. Delay in sending the relevant documents by lending departments after 
identifying the personnel by CBI for deputation.  
iv. Non-identifying suitable/skilled personnel by the lending departments which 
results in non-selection of the personnel even after scrutiny.” 
6.2  The shortage of suitable nominations for deputation to CBI is a serious concern 
affecting its operational efficiency. The primary reasons include manpower shortages 
in lending departments, reluctance of state police forces, procedural delays in 
documentation, and inadequate identification of skilled personnel. These issues lead 
to unfilled vacancies, affecting the agency’s investigative capabilities. The lack of 
incentives for lending departments further discourages officers from opting for 
deputation. Administrative bottlenecks in processing nominations delay appointments, 
impacting critical cases. Addressing these challenges requires institutional reforms, 
streamlined processes, and better incentives to attract and retain skilled personnel. 
 
6.3  To reduce reliance on deputation, the Committee recommends that CBI 
develop an independent recruitment framework by allowing direct recruitment 
for core ranks like Dy.S.Ps Inspectors and Sub-Inspectors through SSC, UPSC, 
or a dedicated CBI exam. It should also introduce lateral entry for specialists in 
cybercrime, forensics, financial fraud, and legal domains. The CBI should strive 

 
57 
to establish a permanent cadre with structured career progression, this in turn 
will help CBI in ensuring long-term stability. An in-house expertise team should 
be constituted which will make it less reliable on outside experts.  Deputation 
may be retained only for select senior positions requiring diverse experience, but 
streamlining recruitment procedure and reforms will help CBI in enhancing  
operational efficiency and investigative capabilities. 
  
Case Management System 
6.4 The Committee in para 6.13 of its 126th Report had stressed the need for 
greater transparency in CBI’s functioning by publishing case statistics and its Annual 
Report online. It had recommended establishing a Centralized Case Management 
System to track case progress, ensuring public accessibility. This will enhance 
accountability, efficiency, and citizen empowerment, making CBI’s operations more 
transparent and responsive. The Department in its Action Taken Note responded as 
stated below :-   
 “ Investigation is carried out as per provisions of law.  Upon 
completion of the investigation, all the relevant documents pertaining to 
the case, filed along with the final report, are available in Courts.  
Besides, brief of important registration, searches, arrests, filing of 
charge-sheet, conviction etc., are available in Media column of CBI 
Website, which is accessible to all. So far as maintaining a case 
management system in CBI, it is to be intimated that the same under 
implementation. Sharing of progress to public may be pre-judicial to 
investigation.  Regarding placing CBI Annual Report on its website, it is 
submitted that Annual Report, as of now, being submitted to CVC, MHA, 
DOPT, Parliamentary Standing Committee etc.” 
6.5 The Department’s response highlights the legal constraints on disclosing case 
details. While investigation documents are available in courts, accessing them remains 
cumbersome for the public. The media section in CBI website provides only selective 
updates, which do not substitute for structured public reporting. The implementation 
of a Case Management System is a positive step, but concerns about public access 
remain unresolved. Further, restricting the CBI Annual Report to select government 

 
58 
bodies limits broader transparency. The Committee believes that structured, non-
prejudicial disclosures can enhance public trust while maintaining investigative 
integrity. 
6.6 The Committee emphasizes the need for greater transparency in 
functioning of CBI by making case statistics and the Annual Report publicly 
available on its website. The Centralized Case Management should allow public 
access to non-sensitive case details which will enhance accountability, efficiency, 
and trust in operations of CBI. The Committee believes that proactive disclosure 
of information will also empower citizens while ensuring responsible governance. 
The Committee urges CBI to implement these measures swiftly, balancing 
investigative confidentiality with the public’s right to information for a more 
transparent and responsive system.  
Delhi Special Police Establishment Act: 
6.7  The Committee in para 6.17 of its 126th Report had recommended for enacting 
a new law to redefine CBI’s status, functions, and powers, addressing limitations in 
the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act. The new law was supposed to provide 
clear legal authority, safeguards for impartiality, and uniform jurisdiction, ensuring 
CBI’s effective and independent functioning, especially as nine states had withdrawn 
general consent for investigations. The Department in its Action Taken Note with 
respect to the recommendation responded as stated below :-   
 “Power of CBI to investigate emanates from the Delhi Special Police 
Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946. 
As per Section 6 of the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946, Central 
Bureau of Investigation (CBI) needs the consent from the respective State 
Government for conducting investigation in its jurisdiction. In terms of 
the provision of Section 6 of the DSPE Act, 1946, the State Governments have granted 
a general consent to CBI for the 
investigation of specified class of offences against specified categories of persons 
enabling CBI to register and investigate those specified matters. 
For investigation of any matter in such State, which is not covered in the aforesaid 
consent, specific consent of State Government is required for the CBI to investigate in 
the State. CBI seeks such consent on case to case basis.” 

 
59 
6.8  The response of Department merely states the existing legal framework 
under the Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946, without addressing the 
Committee’s core concern—the need for a new legal framework to strengthen CBI’s 
autonomy and effectiveness. The current requirement of state government consent 
creates operational challenges, especially as currently eight states have withdrawn 
general consent, limiting CBI’s jurisdiction and investigative efficiency. The absence 
of a uniform legal mandate undermines its ability to function as an independent agency. 
The Committee believes that a comprehensive legal overhaul is essential to ensure 
clarity, consistency, and impartiality in CBI’s investigations across India. 
6.9 The Committee notes that eight states have withdrawn general consent 
for CBI investigations limiting severely its ability to investigate corruption and 
organized crime. To address this problem, the Committee feels a separate/new 
law granting CBI wider investigative powers without state consent for cases 
affecting national security and integrity may be enacted by taking views also 
from State Governments. The law should also include safeguards to ensure 
impartiality, preventing state governments from feeling powerless. This reform 
is essential to ensure timely and unbiased investigations, prevent delays which 
will not undermine public trust. The Committee urges action on this front which 
will strengthen the authority of CBI keeping in view the federal balance.

time updates through a dashboard. This system enables senior officers to monitor 
complaints at various stages, such as pending investigation, examination for First

6.13 The Department informed the Committee that some of the challenges faced by 
the competent authorities in granting sanction under the PC Act, 1988 are delay in 
submission of views of concerned administrative authorities and non-availability of 
relevant records required for taking a decision for granting sanction for prosecution. 
Commission has advised in its Vigilance Manual for organizations to keep attested 
copies of the documents provided to Law Enforcement Agencies (LEA) which may 
be required later by the Competent Authority for deciding on request for prosecution 
sanctions. 

 
61 
6.14 The Committee observes that delays in granting sanction for prosecution under 
the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, arise mainly due to the slow submission of 
views by administrative authorities and the non-availability of relevant records. These

deterrence. The Commission’s advisory in the Vigilance Manual, recommending 
organizations maintain attested copies of documents shared with Law Enforcement 
Agencies (LEAs), is a step towards addressing this issue. However, strict enforcement 
of this practice, digital record-keeping, and better interdepartmental coordination are

departmental coordination mechanism should be introduced to expedite 
document sharing. Training programs must be conducted to ensure vigilance 
officers and administrators adhere to streamlined sanction procedures. 
Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) 
 
Single Bench mechanism for pension-related & senior citizen related cases 
6.16 The Committee has been informed that pension cases generally involve 
straight forward legal and factual issues, making them suitable for single-member 
adjudication. This helps to optimize workload and allocate more resources to complex 
cases that require a Division Bench. Single-Member Benches handle such pension 
matters effectively and it ensures quicker adjudication. 
6.17 It has further been informed that CAT benches deal with a large number of 
service-related issues including pension matters. By identifying the pension related 
members as single-member matters, the Tribunal ensures clearance of pending cases 
faster, reducing overall backlog. The measure helps to ensure that the grievances of 
the retired employees are redressed in a timely manner, especially when the 

 
62 
availability of Division Bench is limited due to leave/ vacancy of Members in 
different Benches. 
  
6.18 As per latest data (as on 31.01.2025) pertaining to the institution and disposal 
of pension and senior citizen related cases for the period from 2019-2025 shared with 
the Committee, a total of 6,468 pension related cases were instituted, whereas the 
disposal figure of such cases stood at 6,464 over the ibid period. Further, a total of 
28,648 senior citizen related cases were instituted over the relevant period and the

6.19 The Committee notes that the adoption of Single-Member Benches for pension 
cases has proven effective in optimizing workload management within the Central 
Administrative Tribunal (CAT). Given the straightforward legal and factual nature of 
pension disputes, this approach ensures faster adjudication and minimizes case 
backlogs. The data suggests near-parity in the institution and disposal of pension 
cases, demonstrating efficiency. However, the significant gap in senior citizen-related 
case disposal indicates the need for further reforms. Expanding Single-Member 
adjudication to other straightforward service matters and enhancing resource 
allocation could further reduce backlogs and improve grievance redressal for retirees 
and senior citizens. 
6.20 The Committee recommends that to enhance efficiency, the Tribunal 
should institutionalize a permanent framework for Single-Member Benches in 
all pension-related and other straightforward service matters. A fixed timeline of 
90 days for case disposal should be introduced, with periodic monitoring to 
ensure adherence. Additionally, digital case management tools should be 
deployed for tracking pending senior citizen cases, prioritizing those pending for 
extended periods.

6.31 The Department informed the Committee that constitution of the inquiry wing

and resolution of backlog vacancies.  The Committee feels by following this 
approach, reserved category vacancies may get reduced to a large extent.        
(para 3.7) 
 
12. The  Committee, therefore, recommends that a Monitoring Mechanism 
may be established to ensure timely filing of IPRs by all IAS officers. This 
mechanism should involve creation of a dedicated task force within the 
Department responsible for tracking and filing status of all officers. Additionally, 
the Committee proposes to introduce penalties or corrective actions for non-
compliance, including automatic escalation procedures for officers who fail to 
file their IPRs despite reminders. This will strengthen accountability and ensure 
timely filing, making the process more robust and ensure greater adherence to 
the requirements. 
(para 3.15) 
13. All organs of the Government of India are taken care of mainly by 
Central Secretariat Services (CSS) & Central Secretariat Stenographers’ 
Services (CSSS). They are the mainstay of Central Secretariat working.  It has 
been brought to the notice of the Committee that especially in CSS & CSSS all 
gazetted officers are rotated on the basis of sensitive and non sensitive postings 
and at sensitive places officers are replaced after tenure of 3 years.  Similarly 
Ministries have also been categorized as economic and non-economic.   The 
Committee notes that there has been a rotational policy for all officers but is not 
being implemented in toto and there are officers who are on potentially favorable 
Ministries/places for over 8-9 years, especially in economic and sensitive 
Ministries and are continuing their stay despite head of organizations been 
replaced 4-5 times. The Committee feels that this trend should be assessed. 
Longer stays at particular seats/places breeds corruption and remedial measures 
needs to be taken immediately and all transfers should be made immediately as 
per policy and no officer should stay beyond the prescribed time limit in any 
Ministry.  Secondly, the Committee wishes to point out that the Ministry of 
Finance has three department which have been categorized as economic and non 
economic, instances have come to the notice of the Committee that there are 

 
73 
instances where officers have manoeuvred their postings in such a way that their 
whole career has been in the same Ministry and hence such lacuna needs to be 
plugged without any delay. 
(para 3.16) 
RECRUITMENT INSTITUTIONS 
14.  UPSC informed the Committee that it publishes the preliminary 
examination answer key only after completing the entire selection process. This 
delays candidates' ability to challenge potential errors before advancing to the 
next stage, undermining transparency and fairness. Such a practice can 
demoralize candidates and raise concerns about the validity of the examination. 
Despite rigorous scrutiny, the possibility of errors in the answer key cannot be 
entirely ruled out. To enhance credibility, fairness, and candidate confidence, the 
Committee reiterates its recommendation contained in para 4.5 of its 126th 
report that UPSC may explore and take steps to release the answer key 
immediately after the preliminary examination and provide candidates with an 
opportunity to raise objections before proceeding further.   
(para 4.6) 
 
15.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should set a 
clear timeline for implementing the Baswan Committee recommendations. A 
dedicated team can be formed to prioritize key issues such as answer key 
disclosures and examination structure. Additionally, stakeholder consultations, 
including candidates and subject experts, may be conducted for effective and 
visible reforms. Regular progress updates should be published to maintain 
transparency and accountability. If any of the recommendations require policy 
changes, then they should be escalated for prompt government approval. A 
structured implementation roadmap will help modernize the UPSC examination 
process while addressing concerns about fairness, transparency, and efficiency. 
(para 4.10) 
 
16.  SSC submitted that without empirical data, it is unclear whether 
reinstating descriptive tests, either in CBT mode or traditional format, would 

 
74 
affect the recruitment cycle. A detailed assessment is necessary to evaluate 
whether descriptive evaluations enhance candidate selection without causing 
delays in the hiring process. The Committee, therefore, recommends to conduct a 
comprehensive study on the impact of descriptive tests on recruitment 
effectiveness, selection quality, and process efficiency. This study should compare 
recruitment outcomes before and after their discontinuation, assessing whether 
descriptive evaluations improve candidate competency for management posts. 
Based on the study, if reintroduction proves beneficial, a hybrid approach—
combining objective tests with limited descriptive components—could be piloted.  
(para 4.14) 
17.   The Committee appreciates that NRA has conducted a study on 
recruitment systems across Central and State agencies to identify challenges in 
implementing the Common Eligibility Test (CET). However, the findings may 
emphasize the need for a structured, transparent, and efficient examination 
framework in place at the earliest. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the department should expedite the finalization and implementation of 
standardized Norms, Standards, and Guidelines for CBT to ensure uniformity, 
fairness, and security in recruitment exams. A phased rollout of the Common 
Eligibility Test (CET) should be piloted across select regions before its 
nationwide implementation to assess the efficiency and address potential 
challenges. Additionally, NRA should also establish a grievance redressal 
mechanism for handling candidate concerns and for ensuring transparency. 
(para 4.19) 
18.  The Committee reiterates its concern over the significant gender gap in 
top managerial positions within CPSEs, where women constitute only 7% of the 
eligible pool and merely 7% at the Board level. Emphasizing that gender 
equality is crucial for an inclusive and accountable public administration, in line 
with the Government’s Nari Shakti policy, the Committee once again 
recommends that the Department, being the nodal agency for personnel 
management, must thoroughly examine the factors leading to the 
underrepresentation of women in leadership roles and implement concrete 
measures to eliminate barriers hindering their advancement.  

 
75 
(para 4.23) 
 
TRAINING INSTITUTIONS 
19. As per the information provided to the Committee, ISTM has been facing 
an acute shortage of staff –both faculty and non-faculty officers in the past few 
years due to a variety of reasons.   ISTM has a total sanctioned strength of 95 out 
of which 29 posts are vacant. The Committee recommends Department to take 
immediate steps to fill up the vacant posts in ISTM as shortage of staff impacts 
the effective functioning of the institution.   
(para 5.7) 
 
20. To a specific question about setting up of a study group to suggest 
reforms in the training imparted to civil servants, the Committee was informed 
that no specific Committee/ Panel/ study group to suggest reforms in the training 
imparted to civil servants at LBSNAA in the last five years have been set up by 
the Government of India. Though some changes may have been affected in the 
system of training during this period, but the time is evolving at a fast pace and 
training to civil servants requires alignment with the pace of time.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should establish the 
National Committee on Civil Services Training Reforms (NCCSTR) to 
modernize civil servant training. Led by a senior bureaucrat, it should include 
experts from governance, academia, industry, and international institutions. Key 
focus areas may include AI and digital governance, experiential field learning, 
ethical leadership, crisis management, and global best practices. The committee 
may submit initial recommendations in 6 months and a final report in 12 
months, with pilot implementation at LBSNAA. This will ensure future-ready, 
citizen-centric, and effective governance, enhancing the capability of civil 
servants to address evolving administrative challenges.  
(para 5.8) 
INTEGRITY, VIGILANCE, TRANSPARENCY AND SERVICE 
MATTERS 
 

 
76 
21. To reduce reliance on deputation, the Committee recommends that CBI 
develop an independent recruitment framework by allowing direct recruitment 
for core ranks like Dy.S.Ps, Inspectors and Sub-Inspectors through SSC, UPSC, 
or a dedicated CBI exam. It should also introduce lateral entry for specialists in 
cybercrime, forensics, financial fraud, and legal domains. The CBI should strive 
to establish a permanent cadre with structured career progression, this in turn 
will help CBI in ensuring long-term stability. An in-house expertise team should 
be constituted which will make it less reliable on outside experts.  Deputation 
may be retained only for select senior positions requiring diverse experience, but 
streamlining recruitment procedure and reforms will help CBI in enhancing  
operational efficiency and investigative capabilities. 
(para 6.3) 
 
22. The Committee emphasizes the need for greater transparency in 
functioning of CBI by making case statistics and the Annual Report publicly 
available on its website. The Centralized Case Management should allow public 
access to non-sensitive case details which will enhance accountability, efficiency, 
and trust in operations of CBI. The Committee believes that proactive disclosure 
of information will also empower citizens while ensuring responsible governance. 
The Committee urges CBI to implement these measures swiftly, balancing 
investigative confidentiality with the public’s right to information for a more 
transparent and responsive system.  
(para 6.6) 
 
23. The Committee notes that eight states have withdrawn general consent 
for CBI investigations limiting severely its ability to investigate corruption and 
organized crime. To address this problem, the Committee feels a separate/new 
law granting CBI wider investigative powers without state consent for cases 
affecting national security and integrity may be enacted by taking views also 
from State Governments. The law should also include safeguards to ensure 
impartiality, preventing state governments from feeling powerless. This reform 
is essential to ensure timely and unbiased investigations, prevent delays which 

 
77 
will not undermine public trust. The Committee urges action on this front which 
will strengthen the authority of CBI keeping in view the federal balance.  
(para 6.9) 
 
 
24. The Committee recommends periodic review on the effectiveness of 
Vigilance Case Monitoring System (VCMS) and based on it, improvements 
should be made. An oversight committee may be formed comprising 
representatives from the Central Vigilance Commission, CBI, vigilance 
departments, and technical experts. It should focus on reducing delays by setting 
clear timelines for case resolution, improving inter-agency coordination, and 
leveraging AI for case prioritization. This committee should also ensure user 
training and address any technical challenges faced by stakeholders. 
Additionally, it should submit bi-annual reports highlighting systemic issues and 
suggesting policy reforms to enhance efficiency and effectiveness of the vigilance 
framework.  
(para 6.12) 
 
25.  The Committee recommends that a Centralized Digital Case Repository 
(CDCR) should be established by the Central Vigilance Commission to store 
attested copies of all documents submitted to Law Enforcement Agencies 
(LEAs). Competent Authorities must be given secure access to retrieve case 
records instantly. A mandatory timeline may be in place/implemented for 
administrative authorities to submit their views on prosecution sanctions, with 
accountability measures for delays. Regular audits should be conducted to 
ensure compliance with record-keeping protocols.  Further, an inter-
departmental coordination mechanism should be introduced to expedite 
document sharing. Training programs must be conducted to ensure vigilance 
officers and administrators adhere to streamlined sanction procedures.  
(para 6.15) 

 
78 
 
26. The Committee recommends that to enhance efficiency, the Tribunal 
should institutionalize a permanent framework for Single-Member Benches in 
all pension-related and other straightforward service matters. A fixed timeline of 
90 days for case disposal should be introduced, with periodic monitoring to 
ensure adherence. Additionally, digital case management tools should be 
deployed for tracking pending senior citizen cases, prioritizing those pending for 
extended periods.  
(para 6.20) 
 
27. The Committee recommends that to ensure the timely completion of 
digitization and full implementation of Advance Case Information System 
(ACIS) in CAT, e-Courts/Smart Courts which are yet to be made fully functional 
under ACIS, needs to be made operational. The DMS should be tested 
rigorously, with feedback loops from judicial officers and litigants to ensure 
user-friendliness. Training programs should be conducted for court staff to 
enhance digital adoption. A performance review mechanism should be 
introduced to assess the impact of ACIS on case disposal rates and recommends 
further technological enhancements for efficiency.  
(para 6.25) 
 
28. The information provided indicates that the CAT Kolkata Bench is 
functioning from the CGO Complex, occupying 23,789 sq. ft., with a monthly 
license fee of ₹8,56,404. While the current arrangement meets operational needs, 
long-term financial implications should be considered. Renting space indefinitely 
results in recurring costs without asset creation. Constructing a dedicated 
building would ensure financial prudence, institutional stability, and better 
infrastructure customization. Therefore, the Committee recommends that a 
feasibility study be conducted to assess the cost-benefit of constructing a 
permanent building. If viable, necessary budgetary allocations should be made to 

 
79 
initiate the project in a phased manner, ensuring cost efficiency while 
maintaining uninterrupted functioning of the Bench.  
(para 6.27) 
29.    The Committee recommends that workforce shortages in the CIC 
should be addressed. The revival of deemed abolished ASO and MTS posts 
should be prioritized through urgent approvals.   CIC should coordinate with 
SSC for filling vacant ASO, SA, and Stenographer posts and completing the 
recruitment process within a specified timeframe. Further, a workforce planning 
framework should be introduced to anticipate future vacancies and streamline 
recruitment cycles.  
(para 6.30) 
 
30. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department may take 
urgent steps to constitute the Inquiry and Prosecution Wings of Lokpal, 
preferably within a period of six months. The structure, staffing, and jurisdiction 
of these wings should be well defined. Recruitment of qualified personnel, 
including investigators, legal experts, and prosecutors, may be given top priority. 
Until these wings become fully operational, a dedicated coordination mechanism 
may be set up with CVC and CBI to streamline the ongoing cases. 
(para 6.33) 
31. The Committee recommends that a structured mechanism should be 
introduced to ensure timely submission of comments by public servants and 
competent authorities for timely completion of preliminary inquiries under the 
Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013. A fixed timeline may be enforced strictly for 
response submission, with automatic escalation for non-compliance. Digital 
platforms should be implemented for secure and real-time submission of 
comments to minimize procedural delays. A dedicated monitoring unit within 
the Lokpal may track compliance, issue reminders, and report persistent delays.  
(para 6.36)

  I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice, having been authorized by the Committee to 
submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this One Hundred Forty Six Report on 
Demands for Grants 2025-26 pertaining to the Department of Administrative Reforms & 
Public Grievances and Department of Pension & Pensioners' Welfare (Ministry of Personnel, 
Public Grievances & Pensions).

Reforms & Public Grievances and Department of Pension & Pensioners' Welfare vis-à-vis 
expenditure made out of Consolidated Fund of India.

DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND  
PUBLIC GRIEVANCES (DARPG) 
Evolution of the Department 
1.3 In March, 1954, an Organisation and Method (O & M) Division was set up in Cabinet 
Secretariat as a follow up to one of the recommendations made by Paul H. Appleby. In 
March, 1964, a Department of Administrative Reforms was set up within the Ministry of 
Home Affairs and Organisation and Method (O & M) Division was transferred to its charge 
from the Cabinet Secretariat. On 7th February, 1973, the work relating to the Department of 
Administrative Reforms was transferred to Department of Personnel created under Cabinet 
Secretariat on 1st August, 1970 and was re-designated as Department of Personnel and 
Administrative Reforms. In April, 1977, the Department of Personnel and Administrative 
Reforms was shifted from Cabinet Secretariat to the Ministry of Home Affairs. In March 
1985, the Department of Personnel and Administrative Reforms was elevated to a full fledged 
Ministry of Personnel and Training, Administrative Reforms, Public Grievances and 
Pensions. On 10th December, 1985 Ministry of Personnel and Training, Administrative 
Reforms, Public Grievances and Pensions was re-designated as the Ministry of Personnel, 
Public Grievances and Pensions with three Departments namely, Department of Personnel 
and Training (DOPT), Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances and 
Department of Pension and Pensioners Welfare.  The Ministry was placed under the overall 
charge of the Prime Minister assisted by a Minister of State. 
About the Department 
1.4 The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances is the nodal 
agency of the Government of India for administrative reforms as well as for redress of public 
grievances relating to the States in general and grievances pertaining to Central Government 
agencies in particular. The Department disseminates information on important activities of 
the Government relating to administrative reforms and public grievance redressal through 
publications and documentation. The Department also undertakes activities in the field of 
international exchange and cooperation to promote public service reforms. There are 8 
Divisions in the Department namely Administrative Division, Administrative Reforms (AR) 
Division, Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC) Division, Documentation And 
Dissemination (D&D) Division, e-Governance (e-Gov) Division, International Exchange & 
Cooperation (IE&C) Division,  Organization & Method (O&M) Division, Public Grievances 
(PG) Division. The Department comes under the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances 
and Pensions and is headed by a Secretary.  
 
 
 

 11 
Functions of the Department 
1.5 As per the Government of India Allocation of Business Rules, the following subjects 
have been allocated to the Department of Administrative Reforms & Public Grievances: 
(i) Administrative Reforms, including e-governance and dissemination of best 
 practices. 
(ii) Organization and Methods. 
(iii) Policy, coordination and monitoring of issues relating to: 
(a)  Redress of public grievances in general; and 
(b)  Grievances pertaining to Central Government agencies. 
(iv) (a)  Research in public management; 
       (b)  Liaison with State Governments, professional institutions etc. in public 
  management matters. 
(v) Administration of Central Secretariat Manual of Office Procedure.  
 
 
MAJOR ACTIVITIES / INITIATIVES OF THE DEPARTMENT 
Public Grievances 
1.6 An online system for grievance redress, called the ‘Centralized Public Grievance 
Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS) has evolved since 2007. The Department 
extensively uses this System to forward public grievances to the Central Government 
Ministries/Departments/Organisations as well as to the State Governments concerned. 
 1.7 Public grievance mechanism of PMO, the President’s Secretariat, the Directorate of 
Public Grievances (Cabinet Secretariat), Department of Administrative Reforms & Public 
Grievances (DARPG) and that of Department of  Pension & Pensioners’ Welfare portal are 
integrated through CPGARMS thus enabling grievances lodged to any of these entities to be 
transferred to the Central Ministries/Departments and to the State / UT Governments online 
through CPGRAMS.  
Introduction of an Appeal Mechanism/functionality in CPGRAMS 
1.8 Centralized Public Grievances Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS) is one 
of the most widely used IT platforms, provides a direct access to the citizens to the 
government authorities. Citizens can file and track their grievances in CPGRAMS 24x7. All 
Ministries/ Departments of GOI and State Governments are part of this system.  The Appeal 
provision is made for redressal of dissatisfied grievances identified through a mandatory 
feedback rating to be given by the Citizen on disposal of the grievance by the Nodal 
Grievance Officers. 
  

 12 
Citizens' Charter 
1.9 A Citizens' Charter represents the commitment of the Organisation towards standard, 
quality and time frame of service delivery, grievance redress mechanism, transparency and 
accountability. Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances, in the Ministry 
of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, Government of India, in its efforts to provide 
more responsive and citizen-friendly governance coordinates the efforts to formulate and 
operationalise Citizens' Charters. Various Central Government Ministries/ Departments/ 
Organisations have brought out their Citizens' Charters. With a view to ensure effective 
implementation of Citizens' Charter, Nodal Officers have been appointed in the concerned 
Central Government Ministries/ Departments/ Organisations.   
Sevottam 
1.10 Sevottam is a generic framework for achieving excellence in public service delivery. 
It comprises of 3 modules namely, Citizen’s Charter, Grievance Redressal Mechanism and 
Capability Building for Service Delivery. As part of the Strategic plan for Capability 
Building towards implementing Sevottam Quality Management System, a Scheme for 
Strengthening of Administrative Training Institutes has been implemented during the  
12th Five Year Plan 2012-2017 in 10 States.  This Scheme was extended for a further period 
of 3 years till 31.03.2020 and for another period of a year upto 31.03.2021.  The Scheme is 
presently under review in the Department.   
e-Office - Mission Mode Project  
1.11 e-Office is one of the Mission Mode Projects approved by the Cabinet under e-
Governance Plan (NeGP). The project is aimed at significantly improving the operational 
efficiency of Central Government Ministries/Departments through improving the workflow 
mechanism and associated office procedure manuals. The Department of Administrative 
Reforms & Public Grievances is the nodal agency to monitor and facilitate implementation of 
the project. With constant monitoring and support, use of e-office has registered further 
increase with 74 Ministries have migrated to latest version of e-office 7.0. E receipt has 
grown from 32% in 2021 to 94.19% in Dec 2024. Over 80% work of Central Ministries are 
now on e-office.   
Central Secretariat Manual of Office Procedure (CSMOP)  
1.12 DARPG is responsible to bring out manual for office procedure in Central Secretariat. 
This is an important reference document provide much needed guidance to Central 
Secretariat system which saves time and efforts in figuring out processes, reduces possibility 
of mistakes and improves efficiency of employees. The Sixteenth edition of the Central 
Secretariat Manual of Office Procedure CSMOP-2022 was released on 5th August 2022. The 
new edition reflects the changes that have been brought in as a result of exercise of increasing 
efficiency in decision making and special Campaign 2.0. DARPG also brought out the first 
Hindi edition of CSMOP on 31st October 2022 to facilitate Secretariat functioning in the 
Official Language. 

 13 
Increasing efficiency in Decision Making  
 
1.13 Process re-engineering for increasing efficiency in decision making in the government 
is one of critical reforms undertaken by the Government to make the governance responsive, 
accountable and efficient. Delayering. Delegation of powers to lower formulations, 
Digitization and Desk officer system have been identified as key reforms towards increasing 
efficiency in decision making. DARPG is following up implementation and impact of these 
measures in the Central Ministries/ Department. DARPG published the Impact Analysis 
Report based on 3rd party evaluation conducted by Quality Council of India. The study 
revealed that reforms of delayering, delegation, digitization and desk officer system have led 
to defined work allocation, reduced channels of submission and timely decision making, 
embodying the principle of "Minimum Government, Maximum Governance."  
 
Special Campaign on Swachata and reducing pendency in Government offices 
  
1.14 In order to reduce pendency in the government Departments and to institutionalize 
Swachhata, the Honb'le Prime Minister Called for annual campaign for taking up these two 
objectives in mission mode. DARPG is nodal Department to curate and steer the Special 
Campaign across all institutions of the Central Government. DARPG structured the 
Campaign outline, issued the guidelines and coordinated the Campaign.  
Prime Minister’s Award for Excellence in Public Administration and Civil Services Day 
1.15 Government of India observes 21st of April every year as "Civil Services Day 
(CSD)". This is an occasion for civil servants of the country to rededicate themselves to 
citizens and renew their commitment to public service and excellence in work. The function 
is normally organized over two days. The 16th Civil Services Day was organised in Vigyan 
Bhawan, New Delhi on 20th-21st April, 2023, on the theme “VIKSIT BHARAT-
Empowering Citizens & Reaching the Last Mile”.  The Civil Services Day could not be held 
in the year 2024 due to the General Elections. The Prime Minister‘s Awards for the year 2023 
and 2024 is proposed to be conferred on the occasion of the 17th Civil Services Day on 21 
April, 2025.               
National Conference on e-Governance (Annual event)  
1.16 Department of Administrative Reforms & Public Grievances, in association with 
Ministry of Electronics & Information Technology and one of the State/UT Governments, 
has been organizing the National Conference on e-Governance (NCeG) every year since 
1997. This Conference provides a platform to the senior officers of the Government including 
IT Secretaries of State Governments, IT Managers of the Central Government, Industry, 
Experts and academia to discuss, exchange views and experiences of various e-Governance 
initiatives and road ahead.   
 
 

 14 
National e-Governance Awards 
 
1.17 To recognize and promote excellence in implementation of e-Governance initiatives, 
Department of Administrative Reforms & Public Grievances presents National Awards every 
year. The Awards are presented generally during an event of two-days, viz. the National 
Conference on e-Governance. These Awards are being given since 2003.  National e-
Governance Awards 2023 were presented during the 27th NCeG.  Total 16 awards, which 
included 09 Gold, 06 Silver Award and 01 Jury Award, were given in the 5 categories of the 
Award Scheme to Central Ministries/Departments, State/UT Governments, Districts, Local 
Bodies, Public Sector Undertakings and Academic & Research Institutions. The gold winning 
projects were given a cash award of Rs.10 lakh and the silver winning projects were given a 
cash award of Rs.5 lakh. The total award money in the 5 categories/sub-categories given was 
Rs.1.20 crores.  
 
Good Governance Webinar Series  
 
1.18 To disseminate and encourage replication of good governance practices, DARPG is 
conducting National Good Governance Webinar series on a monthly basis from April 2022. 
The themes selected for the Webinars cover various sectors like Health, Education, 
Environment, Sports- Khelo India, Innovation Category, Jal/water management, Public 
grievance redressal, Service delivery etc. Purpose is to highlight the best practices adopted by 
the award-winning initiatives for replication by other States/Districts. District Collectors, 
Secretaries in-charge of Administrative Reforms in the States/Union Territories, trainees 
from national and state level administrative training institutes and senior officials from the 
concerned line department in the States/ UTs/ Districts are invited to attend the webinars. 6 
Webinars have been held till now under the National Good Governance Webinar Series 
2024-25. The Webinar has drawn good response and will be scaled up in the next year.  
 
Good Governance Index (GGI)  
1.19 Good Governance Index (GGI) is a comprehensive and implementable framework to 
assess the state of governance across the States and UTs on identified governance parameters. 
Key objective is to create a tool which can be applied uniformly across the States/UTs to 
assess impact of various interventions made by the Central and State Governments. DARPG 
releases Good Governance Index (GGI) on biennial basis. The first GGI was released in 2019 
and the second GGI was released in 2021. The GGI 2021 evaluated performance of States/ 
UTs on 58 Indicators spread across 10 Sectors. The ten sectors covered are (1) Agriculture 
and Allied Sectors, (2) Commerce & Industries, (3) Human Resource Development, (4) 
Public Health, (5) Public Infrastructure & Utilities, (6) Economic Governance, (7) Social 
Welfare & Development, (8) Judicial & Public Security, (9) Environment, and (10) Citizen- 
Centric Governance. GGI 2025 is proposed to be taken up during the next financial year 
2025-26.

National e-governance Service Delivery Assessment (NeSDA):  
 
1.20 The Department of Administrative Reforms & Public Grievances (DARPG) had 
constituted the National e-governance Service Delivery Assessment (NeSDA) in 2019 as part 
of its mandate to boost the e- government endeavours and drive digital government 
excellence. The study assesses States, Union Territories (UTs), and focus Central Ministries 
on the effectiveness of e-Governance service delivery. NeSDA helps the respective 
governments to improve their delivery of citizen centric services and shares best practices 
across the country for all States, UTs and Central Ministries to emulate. 
 
State Collaboration Initiatives  
1.21 DARPG Provides funds to the State Governments under the Scheme 'State 
Collaboration Initiatives' with a purpose to build collaboration with State Governments for 
improving public service delivery. The Scheme was revised in 2015-16 to include funding for 
replication of PM awarded and National e-Governance awarded initiatives.

NATIONAL CENTRE FOR GOOD GOVERNANCE (NCGG) 
1.22 National Centre for Good Governance was established as an autonomous institute 
under the aegis of the Department of Personnel and Training by upgrading the erstwhile 
National Institution of Administrative Research, Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of 
Administration, Mussoorie. DARPG has been made the Administrative authority for NCGG 
since 08.11.2017.  
1.23 The Centre is envisaged to be the apex think-tank that would guide the Government 
and help in implementing good Governance reforms. It seeks to be a high-level institute for 
research and capacity building to deal with the entire gamut of governance issues from the 
National to State to the local level and in sectors across the Government.  
1.24 NCGG is governed by a Governing Body, under the Chairmanship of the Cabinet 
Secretary, GoI and a Management Committee with the Secretary of the Department as the 
Chairperson.  
Objectives of NCGG 
1.25 Following are the objectives of the NCGG:  
 Conducting Capacity Building Training Programme at both National and 
International level on Public Policy & Governance; 
 To function as a national repository on information on best practices, initiatives 
and methodologies that promote Good Governance, E-Governance, innovation 
& change management within the government; 
 To initiate and participate in action research and capacity building on various 
aspects of regulatory and development administration, public policy, governance 
and public management at National/State & local levels; 
 To advise on key issues in governance and development synergy across various 
Ministries/ Departments of GoI, and State Governments; 
 To promote sharing and replication of innovative ideas and best practices in 
Governance; 
 To interact with national and international organizations, in and outside 
government, engaged in research and capacity building in the above spheres.  
 
Mandate of NCGG 
 
1.26 The mandate of the NCGG is to promote Good Governance by:  
 Carrying out Action Research/ Studies on issues relating to governance. 
 Capacity Building on Public Policy and Governance at both National and 
International level. 
 Organizing consultations, workshops, seminars/webinars & talks to promote 
improved governance. 
 Undertaking initiatives for citizen centric governance.
