INDIA INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION CENTRE (IIAC) 
 
3.36 The India International Arbitration Centre (IIAC) has been established by the India 
International Arbitration Centre Act, a statute promulgated by the Parliament of India. The 
purpose of this enactment is to create an independent and autonomous regime for institutional 
arbitration. IIAC has been declared as an institution of national importance. The dispute 
resolution processes that are in place have a huge impact on the Indian economy and the 
global perception on doing business in India. To this end, the IIAC aims to inspire confidence 
amongst parties (both domestic and international) by providing a neutral dispute resolution 
platform for resolution of commercial disputes through a seamless arbitral process.  
 
3.37 The Chamber of Arbitration, established  by the IIAC, will scrutinise the applications 
for admission to the panel of arbitrators and thereafter empanel arbitrators. The Chamber of 
Arbitration shall consist of experienced arbitration practitioners of repute (at national and 
international level) a nd persons having wide experience in the area of alternative dispute 
resolution. The IIAC has been set up with an overall objective of promoting and developing 
India as a major arbitration hub by facilitating a quick and efficient dispute resolution 
mechanism.  
 
3.38 The current composition of  the IIAC is Justice Hemant Gupta  (Retd.), Former 
Judge, Supreme Court of India as  the Chairperson. Dr. Ajay Sahai, Part-time Member,  Sh. 
Anant Vijay Palli, Part-time Member, Mr. Ganesh Chandru, Part-time Member, Dr. Rajiv 
Mani, Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs, Ministry  of Law and Justice, Member -ex 
officio, Ms. Ranjana Chopra,  Additional Secretary &  Financial Advisor, Department of 
Legal Affairs, Ministry of Law and Justice, Member -ex officio. The recruitment process of 
the Chief Executive Officer (CEO), who is also Member-ex officio has been completed and 
appointment letter has been issued. 
3.39      As on date, the Secretariat of IIAC comprises of the following staff appointed  o n 
contractual basis. One Regist rar, One Deputy Registrar, Two Counsels , One Assistant 
Registrar, One Executive Assistant, One Assistant Registrar (Accounts), One Executive 
Assistant (Accounts), One Private Secretary attached to the office of Chairperson, One 
Private Secretary attached to the office of Registrar, One Private Secretary attached to the 
office of Deputy Registrar. 
3.40      The Committee was informed that IIAC is continuously taking steps for augmenting 
its infrastructure, both physical and ICT related. The arbitration room s, meeting rooms, 
library, cafeteria, lounge and arrangements for the officers and staff of the IIAC are being 
provided so as to make it at par with other International Arbitration Centres of repute 
worldwide and for overall development of IIAC as a major arbitration hub. IIAC 
administers arbitration as per the India International Arbitration Centre (Conduct of 
Arbitration) Regulations, 2023. IIAC has developed a Software for conduct of Arbitration 

 
31 
Proceedings as per above said Regulations which went live o n 25 November, 2024 for the 
smooth and efficient working of the conduct of Arbitration Proceedings through online 
mode. In order to make its services cost effective IIAC with the previous approval of the 
Central Government has made the India International Arbitration Centre (Conduct of 
Arbitration) Regulations, 2023 which provides for efficient and time bound process of 
arbitration including day to day hearings. 
3.41 IIAC offers competitive structure of  Administrative Fees and  Arbitrators Fees in  
comparison with other  reputed national  and international institutions. The Schedule 
appended to the aforesaid Regulations provides for the fees and other charges for conducting 
arbitration under the aegis of IIAC.  
3.42 IIAC has also made IIAC (Conduct of Micro and  Small Enterprises Arbitration) 
Regulations 2024 to  contribute to the  sustainable and holistic growth and development  of 
the Micro and Small Enterprises (MSE) ecosystem by promoting faster and more effective 
resolution of disputes affecting Micro and Small Enterprises (MSE).  
3.43 The Committee was informed that the major challenges faced by the IIAC are the 
requirement of funds and enablement of parties to agree to refer their disputes to the IIAC 
for arbitration. For promoting IIAC administered arbitration as per its regulations, IIAC has 
been taking steps to  promote institutional arbitration. IIAC  has since its establishment, 
conducted various workshops, conferences and seminars for various stakeholders in  the 
arbitration ecosystem and encouraged parties to consider adopting IIAC institutional 
arbitration to enable time bound, efficacious and cost -effective dispute resolution.  With 
larger dissemination of  IIAC's efficient operations and  functioning and the support that  
IIAC provides to  the parties over a period of time can contribute in parties agreeing to 
conduct arbitrations under the aegis of IIAC. 
 
3.44 The Committee notes that  even after establishment of IIAC  many arbitration 
cases are still being conducted outside the country, and not many international cases are 
dealt with. One of the factors that is affecting the IIAC is lack of sufficient funds.   To 
transform the IIAC into a globally recognized premier arbitration center known for its 
efficiency, expertise, and neutrality, the Government may prov ide sufficient budget 
allocation to it . Focus should also be placed on enhancing infrastructure, capacity 
building, and international outreach. Though, the Department has taken various steps 
to appoint 161 Arbitrators of Domestic Arbitration and 51 Arbitrators for International 
Arbitration. Considering the number of cases pending in various courts, the strength of 
Domestic Arbitrators should be increased. The Department may also take steps to 
appoint the most qualified arbitrators to the IIAC panel, so that IIAC can be positioned 
as a trusted and influential hub in global arbitration. 
 
MEDIATION COUNCIL OF INDIA 
 
3.45 The Mediation Council of India as envisioned in the 2023 Mediation Act, is a 
proposed body meant to regulate and improve mediation in India pa rticularly for commercial 
disputes. The Council will focus on commercial disputes, aiming to promote alternative 
dispute resolution methods and reduce reliance on traditional court procedure. 

 
32 
 
3.46  The Department during the presentation before the Committ ee has informed that the 
Mediation Council of India is yet to be established. Proposal for creation of 60 posts for 
Mediation Council of India was sent to Department of Expenditure. DoE has approved the 
creation of 21 posts. The following rules under the Mediation Act, 2023 have been notified in 
the Gazette of India:- 
(i) The Mediation Council of India (Salary, Allowances and other Terms and Conditions of 
Service  of Chairperson and Members) Rules, 2024; 
(ii) The Mediation Council of India (Travelling and o ther Allowances for Part -time 
Chairperson and Part-time Members) Rules, 2024; and 
(iii) The Mediation Council of India (Forms and Manner of Annual Statement of Accounts) 
Rules, 2024.  
Section 31 to 38 of the Act which deals with various aspects of the Coun cil have been 
brought into force vide notification dated 09.10.2023. 
 
3.47 The Department further informed that Section 45 of the Mediation Act, 2023 provides 
for a fund called the Mediation Fund for the purposes of promotion, facilitation and 
encouragement of mediation under the Act, to be administered by the Mediation Council of 
India. The Central Government is enabled under the Section 45 to provide grants to the 
Mediation Council of India which will be credited to the Mediation Fund. Upon 
establishment of the Mediation Council of India, the funds would be provided to the Council 
in terms of the statutory and policy provisions.  
 
3.48 The Mediation Council of India is also enabled to frame and notify various 
regulations to facilitate the creation and impl ementation of a framework for institutional 
mediation in the country. These include regulations for manner of conducting mediation 
proceeding under sub-section (1) of section 15; standards for professional and ethical conduct 
of mediators under sub-section (3) of section 15; conditions for registration of mediators and 
renewal, withdrawal, suspension or cancellations of such registrations under clause (d) of 
section 38 and manner of process of conducting online mediation under sub -section (2) of 
section 30.  Section 38 further enable the Mediation Council of India to lay down the 
guidelines for the continuous education, certification and assessment of mediators by the 
recognised mediation institutes.  
 
3.49 In this regard, it may also be noted that for recomm ending draft subordinate 
legislation under the Act a working group/committee chaired by Shri P. K. Malhotra, former 
Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Law and Justice, was constituted. The 
said working Group/Committee had submitted its report to the Department on 31.08.2023 and 
had recommended draft of the rules and regulations for operationalization of the Mediation 
Act 2023. Once the Mediation Council of India is established, the Council shall thereafter 
take steps for the formulation of regulations, recognition of mediation institutes for training 
and other steps in this regard. 
 
3.50 Further, at present training to Mediators is provided by the Mediation and 
Conciliation Project Committee, Supreme Court of India. NALSA allocates grants to  the 
Mediation and Conciliation Project Committee, Supreme Court of India, to support mediation 
activities including training.  

 
33 
 
3.51  One of the main aim for enacting the Mediation Act and establishment of 
Mediation Council is to promote both pre - and pos t-litigation mediation,  which will 
effectively reduce the backlog of cases in courts. However, the Committee notes that the 
Department is yet to establish  Mediation Council of India. The Committee desires it 
may be expedited, so that the purpose of enacting the Act can be achieved.  
3.52 The Committee  desires that a comprehensive awareness campaign across the 
country, at both the state and district levels, through all possible channels  may be 
launched as many are not aware about its establishment . This cam paign will help in 
knowing the existence of the Mediation Council of India and enable the shift of public 
mindset from a litigation-oriented approach to a pre-litigation mediation mindset.

Observations/Recommendations at a Glance 
 
CHAPTER – II - OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS FOR GRANTS 
 
BUDGET 
1. The committee recognizes that legal representation is essential for the effective 
defense of government interests, but the rising costs call for a thorough review of 
expenditure patterns and potential measures for optimization. Therefore, the committee 
recommends that the department strengthen the pre-litigation process by promoting the 
use of Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) and taking steps to reduce frivolous and 
repetitive litigation. To support this, all government departments and PSUs may review 
all the ongoing cases by setting a team of officers and withdraw those that are weak in 
nature. Additionally, a periodic review of the empanelment and performance of legal 
counsel may also be conducted. (Para 2.8) 
LAW COMMISSION OF INDIA 
2.  The Committee notes that despite the approval of the Constitution of Law 
Commission in September, 2024, the appointment of Chairman has not been made till 
date. This act hinders the effective functioning of the Commission, which plays a crucial 
role in legal reforms and policy recommendation. The Committee, therefore, urge the 
department may take necessary steps to appoint the Chairman and Members of the  
Law Commission at the earliest. In future, a clear timeline may b e desired for 
appointment of Chairman and Members of Law Commission of India. (Para 2.12) 
ITAT 
3. The Committee is pleased to note that ITAT Office at Delhi location has been 
shifted to its own building in July, 2024. While, on other 26 locations they are operating 
from the premises given by the Central Government and other Government bodies and 
on 7 locations from buildings of private owners. The Committee urges the Department 
to take steps to move the ITAT Office from the rented premises either to Governm ent 
premises at the earliest. The ITAT may approach the Department to help in this matter. 
The Department may also consider allocating suitable land and adequate funds to ITAT 
for constructing its own premises at these locations at the earliest. (Para 2.14) 
CHAPTER - III 
ASSESSMENT OF FUNCTIONING OF THE DEPARTMENT 
STAFF STRENGTH IN THE DEPARTMENT 
 

 
35 
4. The Committee notes that nearly 50% of the sanctioned positions in the 
Department have remained vacant for quite some time , across various  grades despite 
the Department taking active steps to fill the vacancies. The vacant posts are crucial for 
smooth functioning of the Department.  The Committee, therefore,  urges the 
Department to expedite the process of filling these vacancies at the earliest . The 
Committee has  been given to understand that a Cadre Review Committee  is under 
consideration of Cabinet, the Committee hopes that it would be approved soon. (Para 
3.7) 
5. In order to improve operational efficiency and for ensuring timely delivery of 
legal assistance and  policy implementation , the committee urges the Department to 
prioritize revision of Recruitment Rules (RRs) as recommended by the UPSC  at the 
earliest. (Para 3.8) 
6. The Committee also acknowledges that the digital revolution has transformed 
the landscape of information sharing  to a large extent . The Committee wishes to point 
out that Indian Legal Service Officers are not making full use of it. The Committee is of 
the opinion that its officers should make use of it wherever possible. (Para 3.9) 
VACANCIES OF NOTARIES 
7.  The Committee welcomes the steps taken by the Department to implement the 
recommendations made by it earlier. The committee further notes that the Department 
has inaugurated a dedicated Notary Portal. With this act, the Committee hopes that the 
process of filling up of remain Notary Positions in various States would be soon 
completed. T he Committee also urges upon the Department  that the amendment to 
Rule 10 of the Notaries Rules may be fast-tracked. (Para 3.15) 
 
ENGAGEMENT OF LAW OFFICERS AND ADVOCATES 
8.  Though the Government has been making efforts to appoint best Panel Counsels, 
many are not forth coming for reasons best known to them, thus it has resulted in not 
getting favourable outcomes in the litigation process. The committee, theref ore, 
recommends a systematic, transparent, and performance -oriented approach  may be 
adopted for selecting legal counsel s. Further, having clear qualification criteria and 
utilizing technology for performance tracking, the appointment process can be made 
more efficient and effective. This in turn will help in reducing  delays and improve 
litigation outcomes thereby ensuring that only the most competent and thoroughly 
vetted legal professionals are selected. In addition, the Department may consider 
implementing a feedback mechanism to evaluate the quality of legal services provided 
by the counsels, in the respective departments.  Based on it, contract renewal criteria 
linked to performance may be introduced. (Para 3.19)

various High Courts, District, and Sessions Courts across states, with the Union of India

CHAPTER - I 
OVERVIEW OF THE DEPARTMENT 
1.0 The Ministry of Law and Justice owes its origin to the Charter Act, 1833 enacted by 
the British Parliament and it is one of the oldest limbs of the Government of India. In 
accordance with the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, the Ministry 
comprises three Departments under the overall charge of the Law and Justice Minister 
assisted by a Minister of State. Each department is administratively headed by an independent 
Secretary. 
 
1.1.  The key mandate of the Ministry includes providing policy support in administration 
of justice; giving legal advice to Government of India and defend Government of India in 
various Courts and Tribunals and draft Supreme and Subordinate form of legislations for 
Government of India, etc. 
1.2. In this report, the demands allocated to Legislative Department (Demand No. 65) and 
Election Commission of India (Demand No. 66) have been analyzed and recommendations of 
the Committee have been made at the end of each heading/sub-headings. 
 
1.3. Legislative Department  acts as a service  provider to the Ministries/Departments in 
drafting of principal legislation and vetting of subordinate legislation. The Department is also 
involved in Drafting of Ordinances promulgated by the President, Presidential Acts for the 
States and the President' s Rule, Presidential Regulations to be made by the President under 
Article 240 for Union Territories, Constitution Orders etc.  
 
1.4. This Department also deals with the matters related to Elections to Parliament, the 
Legislatures of States and Union Territories and Offices of the President and Vice -President.. 
This Department also drafts the Finance Bill to give effect to the financial proposals of the 
Central Government every year, which is undertaken in the Legislative Department on the 
budget proposals being brought before it by the Ministry of Finance.  The Department is also 

 
9 
involved in the Publication of Hindi translation of selected judgments of the Supreme Court 
and High Courts on cases pertaining to constitutional, civil and criminal laws in the for m of 
law Journals (Patrikas).  
 
1.5. Further, Ordinance promulgated by the President of India, Regulation made by 
President of India for Union Territories, Electoral Laws and Electoral reforms, maintenance 
of the updated Central Legislation under Bharat Sanhita (India Code) and authoritative 
translation of Central Legislations and Constitution of India in languages specified in the 
Eight Schedule to the Constitution under the Authoritative Text (Central Laws) Act 1973, 
publication and preparation of standard legal terminology, delimitation of Parliamentary and 
Legislative Assembly Constituencies, etc. are also assigned to the Department under 
Allocation of Business Rules, 1961. The Department also imparts training in legislative 
drafting to Officers of the Union/State Government and UT administration through the 
Institute of Legislative Drafting and Research (ILDR). 
 
1.6. It inter-alia administers Personal laws, Electoral laws, the Indian Contract Act, 1872, 
the Specific Relief Act, 1963, the Evidence Act, 1872, the Indian Trust Act, 1882, the Code 
of Civil Procedure, 1908, the Limitation Act, 1963, the Election Commission (Conditions of 
Service of Election Commissioners and Transaction of Business) Act, 1991, the 
Representation of People Act, 1950 and the Representation of People Act, 1951. It also 
facilitates procurement of Electronic Voting Machine (EVM) for the Election Commission of 
India, Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT) Machines and reimbursement of election 
expenditure to State Governments and UT administrations. 
1.7. Legislative Department does not have any statutory or autonomous body under its 
control. It has two oth er wings under it, namely, the Official Languages Wing and Vidhi 
Sahitya Prakashan, which are responsible  for propagation of Hindi and other Official 
Languages in the field of law. 
(i) Official Languages Wing (OLW): The Official Languages Wing is a 
successor organisation of the Official Languages (Legislative) Commission 
under the Legislative Department and is responsible for preparing and 
publishing standard legal terminology and also for translation of Hindi, all the 
Bills to be introduced in Parliament, all Central Acts, Ordinances, Subordinate 
legislations, etc. as required under the Official Languages Act, 1963. The 
Official Languages Wing is also responsible for arranging translation of the 
Central Acts, Ordinances, etc., into the Official Languages as specified in the 
Eighth Schedule to the Constitution as required under the Authoritative Texts 

 
10 
(Central Laws) Act, 1973. The Official Languages Wing also grants-in-aid to 
various registered voluntary organisations engaged in promotion and 
propagation of Hindi and other regional languages and those organisations, 
which are directly engaged in the publication of legal literature and 
propagation of Hindi and other Languages in the field of law.  
       
 (ii) Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan (VSP): VSP is a wing under the Legislative 
Department, Ministry of Law and Justice. This wing was set up under the 
recommendations of the Parliamentary Committee on Official Languages in 
the year 1968 for promotion and propagation of Hindi in the legal field and for 
this purpose a monthly Hindi law journal for publication of reportable 
judgements of Supreme Court was started under the name and style of 
Uchchttam Nyayalay Nirnay Patrika. Thereafter, in the year 1969, another 
Hindi law journal was started under the name and style of Uchch Nyayalay 
Nirnay Patrika for publication of Hindi version of the judgements passed by 
various High Courts. In the year, 1987, Uchch Nyayalay Nirnay Patrika was 
divided into two Hindi law journals i.e. civil nirnay partika and dandik nirnay 
patrika. In this way VSP is publishing three journals for promotion and 
propagation of Hindi in the legal field. Apart from these three law journals, 
VSP is also publishing standard law text books in Hindi written by eminent 
jurists. This Prakashan is also responsible for sale of official diglot edition of 
Central Acts, Constitution of India, Election Manual, Legal Glossary etc. This 
Prakashan also organizes exhibition and sale of official diglot edition of 
Central Acts, Constitution of India, Election Manual, Legal Glossary, law 
journals etc. and also conducts seminars and workshops for promotion and 
propagation of Hindi all over India. 
 
1.8. The organisational set -up of the Legislative Department includes the Secretary, 
Additional Secretary, Joint Secretary & Legislat ive Counsel, Additional Legislative 
Counsel, Deputy Legislative Counsel, Assistant Legislative Counsel and other 
supporting staff. The work relating to legislative drafting, scrutiny and vetting of 
subordinate legislation have been distributed among variou s Legislative Groups, and 
each group is headed by a Joint Secretary & Legislative Counsel or Additional 
Secretary. The Secretary of the Legislative Department also acts as the Chief 

 
11 
Parliamentary Counsel and the Additional Secretary is in -charge of all sub ordinate 
legislation. 
ELECTION COMMISSION OF INDIA 
1.9. The Legislative Department is the administrative Department for the Election 
Commission of India, an autonomous constitutional authority created under Article 324 of 
Constitution for superintendence, direction, control of elections to Parliament, State 
legislatures, and to the offices of the President and the Vice-President of India.  The 
functions, responsibilities, structure and power of ECI are enlisted in the Articles 324 to 329 
of Part XV of the Constitution of India. Article 324 of the Constitution of India bestows 
electoral powers, duties and functions on the ECI, while Section 14 of the Representation of 
the Peoples Act, 1951 provides for conduct of the elections to constitute a new Lok Sabha 
before the expiry of its current term. 
1.10. The Election Commission of India is a multimember body (since 1993) headed by the 
Chief Election Commissioner, who acts as Chairman of the Commission. The Chief Election 
Commissioner and Election Commissioners a re appointed by the President of India and have 
tenure of six years, or up to the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier. The Commission is 
assisted by Deputy Election Commissioners, Chief Electoral Officers (CEO), District 
Election Officers (DEO) and Electoral Registration Officers (ERO), appointed by the 
Election Commission under Representation of People Act, 1951.  
1.11. It registers political parties and allots symbols to them and ensures inner party 
democracy in their functioning by insisting organizational elections at periodic intervals. 
Political parties registered with the Commission are granted recognition at the State and 
National levels on the basis of their poll performance at general elections according to criteria 
specified by it. It implements Model Code of Conduct (MCC) for smooth conduct of free and 
fair elections. It also observes 25th January as National Voters' Day to encourage young 
electors to take part in election process.  
1.12. The electoral expenses on account of conduct of elections  to the House of the People 
and the State Legislative Assembly are borne by the Central Government and the concerned 
State Government, and case of simultaneous elections, the expenditure is to be shared on 
50:50 basis between Central and the concerned Stat e Government. The initial expenditure is 
borne by the respective State Governments, and on submission of the audited report, the 
Central Government’s share is reimbursed through the Legislative Department.  

 
12 
1.13. The Election Commission has its independent  Secretariat for the work relating to the 
smooth conduct of elections to Parliament and State Legislatures, and t here is an exclusive 
demand (Demand No. 66) i.e. voted expenditure under which budgetary allocation is sought 
for running the activities of Election Commission of India.

Repeal of Obsolete Laws  
 
2.37  The Department in its written submiss ion has stated that the Government, as a part 
of its resolve to bring reforms in the legal system had constituted a two Member Committee 
in 2014 to undertake comprehensive review of laws with a view to remove obsolete and 
redundant laws. On the basis of th e recommendations of the said Two Member Committee 
and the Law Commission, the Legislative Department had identified 1824 redundant and 
obsolete Acts. After due examination and consultations with concerned Ministries and 
Departments, a total of 1562 Central Acts have since been repealed. Presently, a total number 
of 76 obsolete and redundant laws have been repealed in 2023 through the Repeal and 
Amending Bill, 2023 (Act No. 37 of 2023) by the Government of India. Total 1486 obsolete 
laws were repealed since  2014 till the last Demands for Grants . Further, the Twenty -third 
Law Commission of India has been constituted with a mandate inter alia to examine 
review/repeal of obsolete laws. 
 
2.38  As far as repealing of Obsolete laws is concerned, the Committee appreciates 
the work done in this regard  and that 1824 reduntant and obsolete laws have been 
identified to be repealed. The Committee also feels that the laws prevalent in a coun try 
should be representative of the political and social structure  existing at that time. The 
Committee hopes that the department will undertake such exercise of identifying and 
repealing the obsolete laws on regular and continuous basis in future also.

CHAPTER II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES GIVEN BY THE GOVERN-
MENT  
Recommendation/Observation 
2.0 It is the duty of the State to provide access to justice to all its citizens and create jud i-
cial infrastructure to provide efficient, economic and timely delivery of justice. The status of 
judicial infrastructure in the North Eastern States can at best be termed as work in progress 
and a lot of work still needs to be done to meet the requirement at the lower end of the spe c-
trum. It does not augur well for a vibrant and aspirational democracy to have Courts which 
are functioning from dilapidated rented premises with insufficient space and which lack basic 
amenities like toilets, water connection, proper electricity supply, etc. Although, the Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for Development of Infrastructure Facilities for Judicia ry, is a ray 
of hope in otherwise gloomy scenario, it is imperative to enhance the share of North eastern 
States  under the Scheme.  (Recommendation No. i) 
Action Taken 
2.1 The budgetary allocation done for the Scheme every year is required to be distributed 
to all the 28 States and 8 Union Territories.  To take care of the interest of the NER, there is 
mandatory allocation of at least 10% of budgetary allocation for the NE Region. Against total 
allocation of Rs.1051 crore for the scheme in the FY 2023-24, a provision of Rs.111 crore 
was kept for the NE Region.   
2.2 As per the laid down process, in the beginning of the financial year, based on the 
weightage formula as provided in the scheme, the tentative allocation for all the states is done 
and made known to them for preparing their action plan. They are required to seek funds im-
mediately and latest by June, after fulfilment of all the conditions, primary among which is 
the utilization of funds released earlier. However, after June, the release can be made to the 
States w.r.t. their requirements and need. The scheme guidelines provide for allocation of en-
hanced budgetary support to the needy States, having good pace of expenditure, if some other 
States are not in a position to seek their allocated funds and thus some savings are available.  
 2.3 Thus, subject to  the utilization of the funds released earlier and having the need and a 
good pipeline of projects, the NER States can also seek enhanced funds, if available, as indi-
cated in para above. In the FY 2023-24, against allocation of Rs.111crore, on account of 
these provisions, funds to the tune of Rs.130.14 crore were released to the states in NE Re-
gion.  
Recommendation/Observation 
2.4 The revised procedural guidelines fo r release of CSS funds under the new Public F i-
nancial Management System (PFMS) has apparently, slowed down the pace of release of 
funds. Due to stringent conditions attached for release of funds, most of the States are finding 

pg. 10 
 
it difficult to get their quo ta of funds despite having huge requirements for funds for their 
projects both ongoing and new. From the data provided by the Department, 3 out of 8 NE 
States did not get any funds during 2022 -23 due to such norms. The Committee is happy to 
note that the D epartment of Justice has made commendable efforts to ensure that funds are 
released to the states on time and that all of them become PFMS compliant. The Committee, 
however, recommends the Department to approach the MoF to get the guidelines on release 
of funds under the CSS relaxed, wherever the States are facing genuine difficulties in the i m-
plementation of such guidelines.  (Recommendation No. ii) 
Action Taken  
2.5 As per the guidelines of Ministry of Finance regarding the release of funds under the Ce n-
trally Sponsored Schemes in vogue in 2023 -24 not more than 25% of the funds earmarked to a State 
can be released at one go. Release of further instalment can only be done after the utilization of the 
previous funds released to it along with the State matching share. The purpose of these guidelines is to 
ensure efficient utilization of funds and to avoid parking of funds. As mentioned above, the scheme 
guidelines also provide for allocation of enhanced budgetary support to the needy states, having good 
pace of expenditure, if some other states are not in a position to seek their allocated funds and thus 
some savings are available.   
2.6 Fund is released to the States as soon as they reduce their unspent balance (Central share + 
state share lying with them) to  the permissible level. The funds using these procedures are released, 
on need basis and only those States get benefited which have exhausted the funds released to them 
earlier and have the capacity to utilize more funds and have ongoing/new projects to ut ilise the 
funds.   
2.7 The States which are not able to utilize the previous funds, are not provided more funds, so as 
to avoid unnecessary parking of funds at the level of the State Government. In the FY 2022 -23, funds 
could not be released to the States of Nagaland, Tripura and Mizoram, as all these States had unspent 
balance of funds available in their respective Single Nodal Agency (SNA) accounts.   The State-wise 
position is as under: 
 Nagaland: Funds to the tune of Rs.13.27 cr ore were released to the State in the F.Y. 2021-22. 
However, as the State did not utilize these funds, it did not become eligible for release of 
funds in 2022 -23. It was only after utilization of unspent balance of funds, that funds to the 
tune of Rs.4.3925 crore were released to the State in FY 23-24. 
 Mizoram: Funds to the tune of Rs.9.5 cr ore were released to the State in the F.Y. 2021 -22. 
However, as the State did not utilize these funds, it did not become eligible for release of 
funds in 2022 -23. It was only after utilization of unspent balance of funds that funds to the 
tune of Rs.8.855 crore were released to the State in FY 23-24. 
 Tripura: Funds to the tune of Rs.7.74 cr ore were released to the State in the F.Y. 2020 -21. 
However, as the State did not utilize these funds, it did not become eligible for release of 
funds in 2021 -22 as well as in 2022 -23. It was only after utilization of unspent balance of 
funds that funds to th e tune of Rs.40.4869 cr ore were released to the State in FY 23 -24. It is 
relevant to mention that  in F.Y.2023-24, Ministry of Finance was also  approached to relax 
the condition to enable this Department to release more than 25% of funds at one go to the 
States. However, this was not agreed to by the Ministry of Finance.

CHAPTER III 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH COMMITTEE 
DOES NOT ACCEPT THE REASONS GIVEN BY THE GOVERNMENT AND REI-
TERATES ITS RECOMMENDATIONS    
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.0 Apart from general PFMS related issues, the North -Eastern States face other cha l-
lenges in creation of infrastructure due to their remote location, hilly terrain, availability of 
unencumbered land. Also the NE States and other hilly States have a short working season 
which makes movement of men and material difficult over the treacherous terrain and ther e-
by making contract implementation difficult with increased time and cost overruns. Because 
of limited railways connectivity in the region, the cost of transportation becomes much higher, 
leading to substantial increase in cost of material. Other reasons include late receipt of project 
proposals and non-receipt of utilization of certificates from the respective state governments. 
The department should take these factors into account while prescribing the modalities of 
fund release. (Recommendation No. iv) 
Action Taken 
3.1 The Department is aware of the challenges in creation of infrastructure due to  remote 
location, hilly terrain, availability of unencumbered land etc. in North Eastern Region (NER). 
These peculiarities, in addition to problem of short working season, limited railways connec-
tivity, are hindering the creation of necessary infrastructure in the North Eastern Region. The 
Department is committed to releasing funds to all the States, particularly to States in NER as 
and when a particular State has utilized the funds previously released to it. As far as the prob-
lem like high transportation cost leading in NER States, the State contribution has been kept 
at only 10% as compared to 40% in other States in respect of funds sharing pattern under the 
scheme.  
3.2 It is relevant to illustrate an example of State of Arunachal Pradesh. In January 2023, 
against the request of the State seeking around Rs.122 crore for ongoing and new projects of 
Court Halls and Residential Units, after due approvals, a  sum of Rs. 32.38  crore wa s r e-
leased to the State in January 2023.  Thus funds to the tune of Rs. Rs.35.97 cr ore (Rs.32.38 
crore central share plus Rs.3.59 crore matching State share) were available to the State. How-
ever, the State has incurred only an expenditure of only of Rs.13. 26 crore (2023-24) out of 
these funds. Thus, the State could not get any funds in the financial year 2023-24, as it is hav-
ing a huge unspent balance of the previous year and is accordingly not eligible for receipt of 
more central funds. One of the importan t conditions for claiming funds under the scheme is 
utilization of funds released to the State earlier. Thus, speedy utilization of funds by the 
States is a pre-requisite for release of further central funds.   
Further observation 
3.3 The Committee takes n ote of th e reply of the D epartment. The C ommittee also 
understands that there is a n issue of non-utilization of the funds released earlier  in the 
north-eastern states which hinders the release of further installments in the scheme for 

pg. 12 
 
the creation of i nfrastructure.  The Committee further emphasizes that a system of p e-
nalties or incentives may be introduced in the scheme so that States may get motivated 
to improve their financial management practices and ensure that funds are used  fully 
and effectively. This could also create a sense of urgency among the States for  timely 
utilization of funds. 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.4 The funding pattern under the CSS for the 8 North Eastern States and two Himalayan 
states is 90:10 (Center: State). However, in some cases the States are finding it difficult to 
even contribute 10% of the funds leading to delay in completion of projects. Accordingly, the 
Committee recommends the Department to explore the possibility of providing a better deal 
in terms of enhanced allocation of funds and relaxation of spending norms under the Scheme, 
considering the peculiarities of the NE States. It is further recommended that the 10% of the 
state quota may also be relaxed for the NE States subject to subsequent recovery from the 
concerned state, so that the ongoing projects are not stalled for want of such meager amount  
of money. (Recommendation No. v) 
Action Taken 
 
3.5 As already mentioned the basic issue, which hampers release of funds to the States, 
including NER States is non-utilization of the funds released earlier. Also, the funds sharing 
patterns are prescribed by Ministry of Finance for all Centrally Sponsored Schemes across 
various Ministries of Union of India. Further, the primary responsibility of development of 
infrastructure facilities for judiciary rests with the State Government, the contribution of Cen-
tral Government through the scheme is supplementary in nature. For the contribution under 
the scheme being supplementary in nature, 10% of the State share is alrea dy a relaxation in 
comparison to States where the State share is 40%. 
 
Further observation 
3.6 The Committee takes note of the reply of the Department. However, the commi t-
tee reiterates its recommendation and suggests the Department to approach the Mini s-
try of Finance with the recommendation of the Committee and seek relaxation for the 
States of the North-eastern region of the country.  
 
Recommendation/observation  
 
3.7 During the interactions with the Committee, the Kohima Bar Association made a r e-
quest for a separate High Court for the State of Nagaland. The President of Bar informed that 
the States like Tripura, Meghalaya and Manipur which came under the jurisdiction of Gauhati 
High Court in 1971 have now established their own High Courts. However, the State of Na-
galand which has been under the jurisdiction of Gauhati High Court since 1963 does not have 
its own High Court. The Committee feels that there is merit in the demand for a separate 
High Court by State of Nagaland and the Ministry of Law and Just ice must coordinate with 
Ministry of Home Affairs to address the demand. (Recommendation No. iii) 

pg. 13 
 
Action Taken 
3.8 The Chief Minister, Nagaland vide his letter dated 25.06.2021 conveyed the decision 
of the State Cabinet taken on the 07.04.2021 for setting up a separate High Court for the State 
of Nagaland.  The proposal to set up a High Court for the State of Nagaland essentially i n-
volves amendment to the North -Eastern Area (Reorganization) Act, 1971, which mandates 
that the Gauhati High Court shall be the common High Court for the States of Assam, Aru n-
achal Pradesh, Mizoram and Nagaland.   
3.9 The matter is currently under examination, in consultation with the Ministry of Home Affairs. 
 
Further observation 
3.10  The matter of establishment of High Court for Nagaland has been in motion 
since 2021. The North-Eastern States like Tripura, Meghalaya and Manipur which were 
under the jurisdiction of Guwahati High Court along with Nagaland have got their     
respective High Courts established whereas the matter of e stablishment of High Court 
of Nagaland is still under examination. T he Committee recommends that the Depar t-
ment of Justice should expedite the necessary process such as consultation with the Min-
istry of Home Affairs etc. for early set up of High Court of Nagaland.

CHALLENGES IN LOK ADALATS 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1 Lok Adalats are being organized by NALSA and State LSAs for amicable settlement of 
disputes. Though Lok Adalats  are designed to expedite case resolution, they encounter 
challenges due to their limited powers compared to regular courts. They also don't have to adhere 
to any proper procedures. Further, they cannot compel the parties to appear for the proceedings. 
Many times one of the parties does not appear for the hearing and then there is a delay in the 
disposal. Therefore, there is a need to have a relook into the powers and procedures of 
conducting Lok Adalats for making them more effective and efficient. The Lok  Adalats should 
have powers to ensure the presence of parties for finding the scope of an amicable settlement. 
(Para 23) 
Action Taken: 
I. The Lok Adalats are governed under Chapter VI (Section 19 to 22) of the Legal Services 
Authorities Act, 1987. As per Section 19 (5) of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 
the Lok Adalats  "have jurisdiction to determine and to arrive at a compromise or 
settlement bet ween the parties to a dispute". The Lok Adalats are statutory bodies 
established for the purpose of amicable settlement between the parties in dispute. Section 
22 of the LSA Act 1987 states that the "Lok Adalats have the same powers as are vested 
in Civil Court under the CPC, 1908, while trying a suit ... ". Overall, the Lok Adalats are 
based on a participatory approach of dispute resolution and the proceeding in Lok 
Adalats are usually not adjudicatory. 
II. With respect to the issue of delay in disposal becaus e of absence of the parties, it is 
submitted that NALSA regularly engages with the SLSAs to conduct pre -Lok Adalat 
meetings for ensuring the attendance of the parties and consequently increasing the

Recommendation/Observation  
2.1  Further, the Committee expresses its concern on the plight of vulnerable sections,

under the relevant Sections/ Acts in cas e if they have been convicted. A large number of

prisoners as on 31 st December, 2022 had spent less than a year in the prison. Further 
break-up of this data point shows that 32% of the under trial prisoners had spent only upto 
3 months in the prison. This reflects that the majority of the under  trial population in 
prisons is a floating population. 
III. To keep a check on avoidable arrests and imprisonment of accused persons due to 
absence of legal representation, NALSA is augmenting legal services at pre -trial stages 
through the 'Early Access to Justice at Pre-arrest, Arrest and Remand Stage' framework.

focusing on legal aid at pre-trial stages to keep a check on avoidable imprisonment: 
A Suspects provided legal aid at police station 27,521

D Persons provided legal aid at remand stage 1,70,912

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE 
COMMITTEE DOES NOT ACCEPT THE REASONS GIVEN BY THE DEPARTMENT

LACK OF AWARENESS AND LEGAL EDUCATION 
Recommendation/Observation  
3.1  Therefore, empowering individuals through education and creating awareness about their 
rights and the role of legal aid is essential to bridge this informational gap. Accordingly, the 
Committee is of the view that Government may take an extensive mass media campaign to 
educate the eligible population about the legal aid avenues available for them to get justice. (Para 
10)  
Action Taken:  
 
I. It is submitted that National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) is bridging the 
information gap among the eligible population with its ongoing awareness programmes. 
During the year 2023, 3,44,580 physical legal awareness programmes were organized 
which benefitted 3,21,50,1 78 persons. The increase in number of persons availing legal 
services reflects the impact of existing awareness programmes: 
A. The number of persons availing free legal services including legal representation, 
assistance, and advice increased by 36% in the year 2023 (14.9 lakh) in comparison to 
the year 2022 (10.9 lakh). 
B. The number of persons availing legal services at pre-arrest stage, arrest and remand 
stage increased by 30% from 1. 7 lakh in the year 2022 to 2.2 lakh in the year 2023. 
II. NALSA regularly conduc ts legal aid camp -based awareness campaigns across the 
country and has developed a NALSA 'theme song' for media -based awareness on the role 
of NALSA. However, NALSA has not yet ventured into mass -media campaigns at the 
national level. For mass -media campai gns, there will be need of specially qualified 
human resource having experience in media and communications for designing, 
coordinating, and analyzing mass -media campaigns. In order to bridge the information 
gap, it is proposed that NALSA will adopt following two pronged approach: 
A. Strengthening the existing awareness programmes/ campaigns: 
Conducting Pan-India beneficiary category wise targeted legal awareness campaigns, 
as per a fixed calendar/schedule of campaigns. The campaigns would include: 
i. Legal Literacy and Awareness camps: Tailored programs will be developed with 
focused attention on specific subject matters and rights & obligations, and 
processes under related laws. 
ii. Community outreach: Public events/meetings, street plays, etc. by students and 
PLVs. 
iii. On-spot legal services: Legal counselling & assistance camps by engaging 
lawyers (Panel Lawyers and Legal Aid Defence Counsels {LADCs}) with 

 
17 
subject-matter expertise; 
iv. Information Dissemination: Outreach -kits containing flyers, posters, etc. in local 
languages regarding the role of Legal Services Institutions (LSIs) and legal 
services schemes, programmes, etc. will be distributed. 
v. Mobile clinics for remote areas: Utilize vehicle based legal aid clinics for remote 
areas and small communities, including nomadic and semi nomadic communities. 
vi. Student PLV involvement: Encourage University based legal aid clinics for 
conducting follow-up legal awareness and outreach camps in areas in the vicinity 
of their institutions. 
vii. Reporting and Feedback: District Legal Services Authorities (DLSAs) will 
prepare categorized data of the campaigns which will be analyzed at the state 
level by the State Legal Services Authorities (SLSAs) and at the national level by 
NALSA for identifying improvement areas and sharing of good p ractices among 
SLSAs. 
B. Building capacity for "extensive mass media campaign to educate the eligible 
population about the legal aid avenue ": 
i. NALSA will take assistance of a special government agency in designing, 
executing, and analyzing mass media campaign s, from the earmarked funds for 
this purpose. 
ii. Local campaigns will focus on digital and physical dissemination of NALSA's 
Information, Education & Communication (IEC) material such as posters and 
flyers on legal services schemes, eligibility under Section 12 of the LSA Act 
1987, platforms/means for accessing legal services, etc. 
iii. These mass -media and physical campaigns will be synchronized with the 
scheduled targeted campaigns as proposed in part 'A' of the proposed action. 
iv. To enhance the dissemination of th e 'theme song', NALSA will coordinate & 
collaborate with mass -media platforms such as All India Radio, Doordarshan, 
Rajya Sabha TV, Lok Sabha TV, etc. for playing NALSA's theme song. 
v. SLSAs and DLSAs will ensure the widespread distribution of NALSA's theme 
song at public events, market areas, community fairs/carnivals, etc., in the local 
language.

Recommendation/Observation 

 
18

eroding the democratic objective of 'justice for all'. As majority of our population lacks legal

19 
crore for F.Y. 2023 -24 for implementation and operationalizat ion of LADCS Scheme)

Action Taken 
I. There are 42,782 PLVs, out of which 17,765 (41.5%) are female, 235 are transgender 
persons and 24,782 are male, who ha ve been given induction training. In addition to the 
induction training, 7,407 PLVs have been provided special training through various  
capacity building programmes during the last five F.Y. i.e. 2019-20 to 2023-24. 
II. As per the Scheme for Para -Legal Volunte ers (Revised), the PLVs' tenure may be 
extended for more than a year if the Chairperson, DLSA finds the PLV's performance 
satisfactory based on regular review. 
III. NALSA periodically organizes national level programmes for PLVs for recognizing and 
commending t heir performance. The State authorities also regularly organize similar 
programmes at the State level. 
IV. In reference to the issue of providing adequate resources to the PLVs, it may be noted 
that the expenses incurred by the PLVs in performance of their dut ies, including travel 
costs, are reimbursed as per the 'Scheme for Para Legal Volunteers (Revised).' 
V. In reference to the issue of payment and adequate compensation to the PLVs for their 
services, it may be noted that the SLSAs and DLSAs decide the honorar ium for the PLVs 
as per the revised Scheme (referred above). As per the Scheme, revised in the year 2013, 
the honorarium of the PLVs shall not be less than Rs. 250 per day. As of January, 2024, 
the honorarium for PLV in different SLSAs ranges between Rs. 250 to Rs. 1800 per day. 
VI. It is proposed that NALSA will ensure that intensive subject-specific trainings for PLVs 
are conducted at the district level based on their area of work and experience, in 
collaboration with the local organizations and government bodies. Further, SLSAs will be 
asked to ensure that the PLVs are empanelled under all categories as mentioned in the 
revised scheme. 
VII. It is further proposed that the agenda of revising the minimum fee structure for PLVs will 
be taken up in the next Central Au thority meeting of NALSA. In addition, all campaigns 
of NALSA will include awareness about the specific roles of PLVs. Pamphlets and 
posters displaying the details of the PLVs in the district/taluk a along with their subject -
specific roles will also be publicized at relevant public places. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.9 Para-Legal Volunteers (PLVs) remain an underutilized resource despite their 
potential to connect marginalized communities with essential legal services. Their 
effectiveness can be significantly enhanced through expanded roles, targeted training, and 
meaningful recognition. To bridge existing gaps, the Committee recommends training 

 
22 
programs should incorporate digital literacy, mediation techniques, and specialized legal 
skills relevant to local needs. Performance-based incentives must be introduced to motiva te 
consistent excellence, while peer -review mechanisms can foster collaboration and identify 
best practices for replication. Recognizing top -performing PLVs through awards and 
public acknowledgment will further enhance their commitment and inspire broader 
participation, ultimately strengthening the grassroots reach of legal aid services. 
 
MANNING THE NALSA  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
3.10 The Committee notes that NALSA's activities have increased manifold since its inception 
and it is actively engaged in taking the legal aid movement in India to every nook and corner. 
However, its existing sanctioned staff strength of 34 only is too low considering its mandate and 
reach. Accordingly, the Committee recommends the Government to sanction additional 40 posts 
as requested by them. (Para 33) 
Action Taken 
I. It is submitted that NALSA is working on the proposals for creation of additional posts 
for NALSA and Department of Justice will act on it as per due process. 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation  
 
3.11 The Committ ee has repeatedly emphasized the urgency of this issue, but the 
Department's responses have been consistently vague and non -committal. NALSA has 
frequently highlighted this concern during its depositions, underscoring the critical 
need for adequate staffin g to fulfil its expanding mandate. The Committee strongly 
recommends that the Department of Justice provide a clear and actionable timeline 
for the creation and recruitment of the requisite officers and staff in NALSA. Such a 
commitment is essential to ens ure the effective functioning of NALSA and the 
fulfilment of its objective to provide accessible and efficient legal aid services across 
the country.

CHAPTER I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN 
ACCEPTED BY THE DEPARTMENT 
Raising the stature of Notaries in India  
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1 Notaries do not receive any remuneration or pay from the government. The 
only source of their income is the fees they charge from their client. The fees to be 
payable to a notary for doing any notarial act are prescribed under Rule 10 of the 
Notaries Rules, 1956. The prescribed fee is meagre, and it was last updated in the 
year 2014. Thus, there is a need to appropriately raise the fees commensurate with 
inflation so that the notaries can have a decent standard of living. Accordingly, the 
Committee recommends that the government to increase the fee payable to notaries 
and make it inflation-linked. It should be revised at regular intervals, preferably every 
five year. (Para 3.3) 
Action Taken: 
1.2 The recommendation of the Committee has been, in principle, accepted and 
accordingly, Rule 10 of the Notaries Rules, 1956 is being suitably amended to 
rationalize and increase the fees to be charged by the Notaries for various purposes. 
 
Sanctioned Strength of Notaries  
Recommendation/Observation 
1.3 It is the considered view of the Committee that the criteria for deciding the 
sanctioned strength of notaries in a state is very vague and lacks objectivity at all. 
The sanctioned strength of notaries in a particular state should be determined on the 
basis of its population, volume of litigation, economic and commercial activities in 
that state, etc., and it should be reviewed regularly. (Para 3.9) 
Action Taken: 
1.4 The number of Notaries to be appointed by the Central Government in various 
States and UTs has been re-calibrated with reference to the State-wise data of 
population (Census: 2011); Gross State Domestic Product at Current Price for 2021-
22 (Source: RBI); State-wise GST collection for the month of November, 2023 and 
pending cases as on 22.12.2023 (Source: National Judicial Data Grid of Department 
of Justice). The geographical landscape and area of the States have also been taken 
into consideration. Based on these rational parameters, the strength of Notaries to be 
appointed by the Central Government in various States has been revised, vide the 

 
10 
 
Notaries (Amendment) Rules, 2024, notified on 24th February, 2024.  In view of this, 
the recommendation of the Committee stands accepted and implemented. 
 
Use of technology in appointment and notarial work  
Recommendation/Observation 
1.5 Presently, the Notary Portal of the Department of Legal Affairs 
(https://notary.legalaffairs.gov.in/) is used for submitting applications and declaring 
results only. With the advancement of technology, the Department needs to harness 
its full potential for making significant improvements in the appointment process. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends the government make this portal a one-stop 
place for advertising vacancies of notaries, making applications, submitting fees, 
publishing results, and downloading e-certificates of practice. The entire process of 
renewal of the certificate of practice should be made through this portal only. 
Further, the annual returns under rule 14 of the Notaries Rules, 1956, should also be 
filled online through this portal. (Para 3.15) 
Action Taken 
1.6 The Department has launched a new Notary Portal (https://notary.gov.in) on 
3.9.2024.  It provides an online interface between the notaries and the Government 
for various services like submission of applications for appointment as notaries, 
issuance and renewal of Certificates of Practice, change of practice area, submission 
of annual returns, etc.  With the launch of the Notary Portal, the Central Notaries will 
not be required to submit applications/ requests in physical mode.  They can submit 
applications online; monitor its progress; and download digitally signed Certificates 
of Practice from their digilocker accounts.   
  
1.7 The Notary Portal has different modules, to be rolled out in phases. In the first 
stage, module relating to issue of Certificate of Practice to the provisionally selected 
Notaries has been launched. Other modules relating to renewal of Certificate of 
Practice, submission of Annual Returns, change of area of practice, etc will be rolled 
out gradually in a phased manner. 
  
1.8 All features recommended by the Committee are being incorporated in the 
Notary Portal.  In view of this, the recommendation of the Committee may stand 
accepted and complied, when all modules of the notary portal (https://notary.gov.in) 
will go live. 
 

 
11 
 
Diversity in notaries' profession  
Recommendation/Observation 
1.9 On this issue, the Committee feels that notaries' profession should reflect the 
diversity of the State in which they are appointed. This will further enrich the notarial 
profession and the legal system. Accordingly, it is recommended that the government 
should appropriately give representation to SCs, STs, OBCs, Women, Physically 
Challenged, Minorities, etc., in the appointment of notaries. Further, at the 
application stage, the candidate should be asked to furnish their category so that the 
Department maintains category-wise data. Accordingly, the rules may be amended to 
that extent. (Para 3.19) 
 
Action Taken:  
 1.10 In order to ensure proper representation of SCs, STs, OBCs, Women and 
PwBD, the applicants of these categories are required to have lesser experience, 
compared to other applicants. Further, the new Notary Portal will capture category 
wise data. Form I of the Notaries Rules, 1956 has also been amended vide the 
Notaries (Amendment) Rules, 2024, notified on 24.2.2024, wherein provisions have 
been made to capture the data related to SC, ST, OBC, Women, PwBD, etc.  
 
 
 
Change of Notarial Year for furnishing the annual return 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.11 The demand for changing the Notarial Year from calendar year to financial 
year seems logical, and this will help the notaries to synchronize their returns with 
that of Income Tax returns. Accordingly, the Committee recommends changing the 
Notarial Year from Calendar to Financial Year. (Para 3.23) 
 
Action Taken: 
1.12 The recommendation of the Committee to change Notarial year from Calander 
to financial year has been accepted and necessary amendment in this regard is being 
made in the Notaries Rules, 1956. 
 
 
 
  

 
12 
 
CHAPTER II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE 
COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF 
THE REPLIES GIVEN BY THE DEPARTMENT 
 
Appointment of Notaries  
Recommendation/Observation 2.1  The Committee accordingly recommends doing away with interview-based 
appointment of notaries. Instead, the selection should be based on an objective type 
written examination along the lines of the All India Bar Examination (AIBE) 
conducted by the Bar Council of India (BCI). In fact, the Central Government may 
consider using the same examination i.e. AIBE, which is conducted twice a year by 
the BCI, for getting the panel of central notaries. (Para 3.6). Action Taken: 
2.2 The recommendation made by the Committee has been examined and the 
following alternatives are under active consideration of the Government for selection 
and appointment as Notaries: 
(i)         replacing the process of interview by written examination; or 
(ii)        introducing written examination for initial screening of the applicants and 
calling only such applicants who qualify the written examination for the interviews. 
 2.3 Since the appointment of Notaries as per existing provisions of the Notaries 
Rules, 1956 is already in progress, the above alternatives will, however, be made 
effective after completion of the current round of appointment process in the 
remaining States and UTs.   
 2.4 Accordingly, necessary amendment will be made in this regard in the Notaries 
Rules, 1956. 
 
Qualification for Appointment of Notaries  Recommendation/Observation 
2.5 On this, the Committee opines that the 10 years of practice as eligibility for the 
appointment is on the higher side, and it should be reduced to 5 years to attract young 
aspirant lawyers to this profession. At the same time, it should also be made 
mandatory for the applicant to have appeared in at least 100 cases. (Para 3.11) 

 
13 
 
 
Action Taken:  
 2.6 The recommendation of the Committee has been examined and it has been 
decided, in principle, to reduce the experience prescribed for appointment as a Notary 
to 7 years, relaxable to 5 years for SC/ ST/ OBC/ PwBD and Women applicants. 
 Accordingly, a suitable proposal to amend the Notaries Rules, 1956 is being moved. 
 2.7 As regards the recommendation regarding prescribing minimum number of 
appearances in Courts, it is mentioned that presently there is no such requirement of 
appearance in cases for being considered for appointment as a Notary.   It may be 
functionally and administratively very difficult to verify the claims of the applicants 
on this aspect.  Therefore, the present system may continue.  
 
Training of Notaries  
Recommendation/Observation 
2.8 Notaries should be equipped to handle electronic transactions, digital 
documents, and online notarization. For this training of notaries should be made. 
(Para 3.17) 
 
Action Taken: 
2.9 It is proposed to make the Notary Portal user friendly. Further, a detailed 
booklet for the help of the users will also be developed and made available on the 
Notary Online Portal. 
 
Designated areas for sitting of notaries  Recommendation/Observation 
2.10 The Committee recommends the government to ensure designated areas for the 
sitting of notaries in every Court complex from where they can do their notarial work 
in a dignified manner. (Para 3.21) 
 
Action Taken:  
 2.11 The recommendation of the Committee is outside the jurisdiction of this 
Department.  The recommendation of the Committee is being forwarded to the State 
Governments for taking appropriate action on the recommendation. 
 
 

 
14 
 
 
CHAPTER III 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF 
WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT ACCEPT THE REASONS 
GIVEN BY THE DEPARTMENT AND REITERATES ITS 
RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
Renewal of certificate of practice  
Recommendation/Observation 
3.1 Almost all the stakeholders flagged the issue of delay in the renewal of 
certificate of practice. They all brought to the notice of the Committee that there are 
allegations of corruption and misuse of discretion in the renewal process. On the 
renewal process, the Committee think that it is being done only to know about the 
antecedents of the applicant and to ensure that the applicant is alive and nobody else 
is practicing in their place.  The Committee is, therefore, of the view that renewal of 
certificate of practice every five years should be done away with. After their 
appointment, notaries may be allowed to practice till a particular age prescribed by 
the government. As the government has the power to suspend or remove notaries on 
a complaint received against them, this will empower the government to tame the 
erring/defaulting notaries. In order to access the antecedent of the notaries and 
confirm they are alive, the Committee desires that a system like online self-
certification or otherwise may be suitably devised by the government. (Para 3.14) 
 
Action Taken: 
3.2 Several steps have been taken to ensure that Certificate of practice of the 
Notaries are renewed in a timely manner. More than 4900 Certificates of Practice 
(CoP) of Central Notaries have been renewed since January, 2023.  Further, the 
Government has launched a new Notary Portal, i.e. https://notary.gov.in, which will 
enable the Notaries to submit their applications for renewal online after the module 
relating to renewal of Certificates of Practice is made live. The Government is also 
working on replacing the physical CoP by digitally signed CoP, which will also be 
available on Digi-locker.  Incidentally, CoPs to the newly appointed notaries are 
digitally signed and are being issued online and are also available in the Digi-locker 
of the Notaries concerned.     

 
15 
 
3.3 Considering the above, the present system may continue.  However, the 
recommendations made by the Committee have been noted and based on the 
experiences gained after full operationalization of the online system, and after 
stakeholder consultation, further improvement in the system will be brought, so as to 
bring more transparency and efficiency.  After reviewing the functioning of the 
Notary Portal, the possibility of reforming the renewal process by amending the 
Notaries Act, 1952 will be explored.  
 
Further Observation and Recommendation: 
 
3.4 The Committee welcomes the steps taken by the Department to renewal of 
Certificates of Practice on time. However, the core concern regarding 
eliminating periodic renewal still remains unaddressed. The Committee's 
recommendation to allow notaries to practice until a prescribed age, subject to 
disciplinary oversight, aims to reduce discretion. The Government should 
consider this proposal after full portal implementation and if necessary consider 
a statutory amendment to introduce one time certification till the prescribed age 
with periodic self-declaration, ensuring both accountability and procedural 
simplification. 
 
Use of technology in appointment and notarial work   
Recommendation/Observation  
3.5 Additionally, the general public should be provided with a state-wise list of 
public notaries, updated on a real-time basis, for verifying the credentials of notaries.  
The public may also be allowed to raise grievances/complaints against notaries 
through this portal. In the long run, the services of this portal may be extended to the 
States and UTs so that the common public can access central and state notaries in one 
place. (Para 3.16) 
 
Action Taken: 
3.6 Once all modules in the Notary Portal become operational, the Register of 
Notaries, as provided in the Notaries Rules, 1956, will get updated on real time basis 
and will be in public domain on the Notary Portal.  To this extent, the 
recommendation made by the Committee will stand accepted and implemented after 
all the modules of the Notary Portal go live. However, as regards recommendation of 
the Committee regarding raising grievances against Notaries through online portal, it 

 
16 
 
is stated that Rule 13 of the Notaries Rules, 1956 prescribes an elaborate procedure 
for inquiry into the allegations of professional or other misconduct of a Notary.  It 
requires that every complaint shall contain the acts and omissions which, if proved, 
would render the person complained against unfit to be a Notary; and the oral or 
documentary evidence relied upon in support of the allegations made in the 
complaint are subjected to examination and corroboration.  The said Rule further 
prescribes that a copy of the complaint shall be sent to the Notary for a written 
statement in his defence verified in the same manner as a pleading in a civil court.  It 
further provides for inquiry in the matter by the Competent Authority.  Considering 
the complexities involved, implementation of the recommendation of the Committee 
does not appear feasible.  However, in order to expedite disposal of complaints 
against Notaries, the Central Government has designated an Officer of the 
Department of the level of Deputy Legal Adviser as Competent Authority solely for 
the purpose of Rule 13 of Notaries Rules, 1956. 
 
Further Observation and Recommendation: 
 
3.7 While the real-time public availability of the Register of Notaries is a 
welcome step, the non-acceptance of an online grievance mechanism limits 
public accessibility and transparency. Considering the increasing digitalization 
of public services, the Committee is of the opinion that a preliminary online 
grievance submission system may be introduced to streamline complaint intake, 
which can then proceed under the existing Rule 13 framework.  
  
 
 
Notarizing of documents  Recommendation/Observation 
3.8 The notarial work should be modernised and digitised, and the use of 
electronic signatures, stamps, and seals should be encouraged. The notarial records 
and certificates should be stored and maintained in a centralised online database, 
which can be accessed and verified by the concerned authorities and parties. The 
notaries should also adopt uniform formats and standards for their documents and 
certificates. (Para 3.26) 
3.9 The Committee accordingly, recommends the government to ensure that all 
public notaries maintain a digital register to keep records of documents notarised by 

 
17 
 
them. Digitalizing records will help avoid fraud, deceit, and tampering of records. 
The concept of digital signature should be introduced so that records are not 
antedated and to identify such notaries who indulge in fabrication or falsification of 
documents. (Para 3.27) 
 
Action Taken:  
 3.10 Implementation of this recommendation involves developing an appropriate 
software for the works performed by the Notaries. Such software will need to have an 
interface between the Notaries and the Public at large. There will also be a 
requirement of necessary infrastructure at the end of Notaries, in the absence of 
which the entire exercise will be futile. The burden on Notaries for procuring and 
maintaining digital infrastructure and their readiness to shift to digital mode also 
needs to be looked into in greater details. The implementation of this 
recommendation also involves the question of data security and privacy.  Cost of 
digital infrastructure also needs to be weighed in. Further, in order to maintain 
uniformity with the States/ UTs, the availability of digital infrastructure with these 
Governments needs to be looked into.   
3.11 While the Department is committed to bringing transparency and efficiency in 
the system, the implementation of recommendation required further deliberations 
with the stakeholders. 
 
Further Observation and Recommendation: 
 
3.12 The committee is of the opinion that the digitization of notarial records, 
introduction of digital signatures, and maintenance of a centralized database is 
crucial for ensuring transparency and preventing tampering. While 
infrastructure and cost concerns are valid, the lack of a definitive timeline or 
roadmap delays critical reform. The Department should initiate this process 
with willing notaries and pilot states, by providing necessary support and 
training.  
Training of Notaries Recommendation/Observation 
3.13 Thus the Committee is of the view that the notaries should be provided with 
regular training and guidance, and their performance and conduct should be 
monitored and evaluated by an appropriate government/ authority. Also, some ethical 
and professional standards should be laid out by such government/ authority to which 

 
18 
 
notaries should adhere to. Further, any complaints or grievances against the Notaries 
should be promptly addressed and resolved. (Para 3.29) 
 
Action Taken:  
 3.14 The Department has launched a new Notary Portal (https://notary.gov.in), 
which will work as a dedicated platform for all issues related to the Notaries.  As 
regards prescribing ethical and professional standards for the Notaries, it is stated that 
even after appointment as Notaries, they continue to be legal practitioners, and as 
such, are bound by the ethical and professional standards prescribed in the Advocates 
Act, 1961.  Other recommendations made by the Committee has been noted for 
further action. 
Further Observation and Recommendation:

Replies of the Department thereto have been categorized and scrutinized under four chapters 
on the basis of satisfaction of the Committee. These replies have been categorized as

Report. The Committee is satisfied with the explanations advanced by the 
Department and does not wish to pursue those as of now (Total-11).  
Chapter – III:  Recommendations/observations in respect of which Committee has not

7).

Ministry have not been received  
-Nil-

CHAPTER I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN 
ACCEPTED BY THE MINISTRY 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1.  The Committee while extending its appreciation to the Election Commission of 
India for their diligent efforts in conducting free and fair elections in the country and 
recommends that citizens should have greater transparency when it comes to the 
Common Electoral Roll and the integration of Aadhaar with EPIC. However, it is 
important to note that linking Aadhaar with Voter ID is voluntary and not obligatory. 
(Para 1.48)   
 
Action Taken 
 
1.2 Comments of this Department: In this regard, it may be stated that the said 
recommendation pertains to the ECI and they have submitted the comments as 
under:-  
1.3 Comments received from the ECI: “The Commission vide its letter no. 
23/inst/2022-ES dated 04.07.2022 has issued instructions to the CEOs of all the states 
and UTs for starting a programme to collect the Aadhar Number of the existing 
electors. A new Form 6B has been devised for electors who have already been 
enrolled in the electoral roll for providing their Aadhar details voluntarily. Further, 
the process of linking of Aadhaar with voter id has not been started yet. Further, the 
Commission is also considering amendments and modifications to the relevant 
provisions related to linking of Aadhar with Voter ID and enrolment Forms in view 
of Hon'ble Supreme Court's direction in the matter. It has been emphasised that the 
linking of Aadhaar with voter ID should be voluntary and not obligatory.” 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.4.  During discussions, some members of the Committee raised doubts about the 
linking of Aadhaar with EPIC of non-citizens, which led the Committee to suggest 
that the ECI should establish a legal provision or an alternative mechanism to ensure 
that non-citizens with Aadhaar are not included in the voter list. Additionally, citizens 
who have not yet linked their Aadhaar should be assured that they can still exercise 
their legal right to vote. The Committee emphasized the importance of these 
clarifications in addressing concerns related to the implementation of a Common 
Electoral Roll (Para 1.49) 

9 
 
Action Taken 
1.5 Comments of this Department: In this regard, it may be stated that the said 
recommendation pertains to the ECI and they have submitted the comments as under:-  
1.6 Comments received from the ECI: “As per Section 16 of RP Act, 1950 a non-
citizen is disqualified for registration in an electoral roll. Therefore, a non-citizen is 
not allowed to enroll even if he possesses Aadhaar card. Aadhar is not a citizenship 
document. Further, under Section 31 of the RP Act, 1950 making false declaration in 
connection with the preparation, revision or correction of an electoral roll or the 
inclusion or exclusion of any entry in or from an electoral roll is a punishable offence 
with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine or both. 
Hence, there is already legal provision available in the present election law to prevent 
a non-citizen from enrolment. 
1.7 For registration as an elector in an Assembly or Parliamentary Constituency, 
person must not be less than 18 years (on the qualifying date prescribed by law) and 
citizen of India having ordinarily resident in the constituency concerned. 
1.8 Further, vide Commission's letter dated 04.07.2022; it has been made amply 
clear that submission of Aadhaar by electors is voluntary and their names cannot be 
struck off from the electoral database merely because of their inability to furnish 
Aadhaar.” 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.9  The Committee recommends that the Legislative Department and the Election 
Commission collaborate to examine the effects of the delimitation process, especially 
in challenging terrains. The Election Commission lacks the authority to direct State 
Election Commissions or appraise the performance of State Election Commissioners. 
The Committee draws the attention of ECI to the fact that treating all regions in India 
as identical can pose a significant risk. It is therefore imperative to recognize this 
reality and take appropriate measures to address it. (Para 1.55) 
Action Taken  
1.10 Comments received from the ECI: “The recommendations of the Committee 
have been noted for future reference.” 
1.11 Comments of this Department: The recommendations of the Committee have 
been noted for future reference. 
 

10 
 
Recommendation/Observation

from the creation of a Common Electoral Roll through the collaborative participation 
of officials who serve in both the Election Commission of India and State Election

statutory authorization before the Election Commission takes charge of creating or 
managing electoral rolls for State Election Commissions. The Committee suggests 
that States may continue to utilize the electoral roll of the Election Commission until

recommends that the Election Commission of India and the Legislative Department

1.14 So far, Election Commission of India has shared its Electoral roll data with 32 
State Election Commissions.” 
1.15 Comments of this Department: It is stated that the recommendations of the 
Committee have been noted by this Department. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
1.16.  The Committee suggests that the Election Commission and Legislative 
Department collaborate to encourage States to utilize the Election Commission's

(Para 1.57)

1.18 Comments of this Department: It is stated that the recommendations of the
