5.2 The Committee notes that out of 37 sanctioned Group A faculty posts, only 24 are 
filled, leaving 13 vacancies (approx. 35% vacancy). Notably, key academic positions such as 

 
61 
Professors of Management, Law, Economics, and Social Management remain vacant while 
programme volume and complexity are increasing day by day. 
5.3 The Committee, therefore, recommends that all vacant faculty posts, particularly 
in areas such as Law, Management, Economics, Social Management, and Hindi & 
Regional Languages, be filled in a time-bound manner to ensure academic depth, 
continuity and training quality. The Committee further recommends that the Academy 
undertake a structured cadre review to assess whether the existing sanctioned strength 
adequately reflects its expanding mandate under Mission Karmayogi, especially in 
emerging domains such as digital governance, artificial intelligence, climate policy, and 
public finance which may require domain experts. 
5.4 Moreover, during the deliberations, the Committee emphasized that young officers 
must not develop a sense of entitlement and should learn to interact with citizens, particularly 
poor and vulnerable sections, with empathy and humility. The Committee was pleased to note 
that 70 per cent of the Foundation Course focuses on behavioural attributes and citizen 
centricity including role plays and interactions with people from humble walks of life.  
5.5 To strengthen the service ethos amongst civil servants, the Committee 
recommends that LBSNAA should systematically integrate modules on seva‑bhav and 
‘frequency matching’ with citizens, into the Foundation Course, district training and 
mid‑career programmes, with specific practical exercises on dealing empathetically with 
common people, especially the poor, elderly, farmers and vulnerable groups. 
5.6 Further, the Committee observed that a deeper understanding of constitutional values 
and the role of Parliament is essential for nurturing a responsive and democratically aligned 
civil service. During the deliberations, the Committee underscored the need for officer 
trainees to develop a fuller appreciation of the role of Parliament, State Legislatures and 
elected representatives in a constitutional democracy. It was also noted that a perceptible gap 
is sometimes felt between elected representatives and the civil services, which could be 
bridged through greater institutional sensitization during training. The Committee also felt 
that a structured exposure to constitutional provisions, Constituent Assembly Debates and 
significant Parliamentary debates would help officers better understand legislative intent and 
democratic accountability. 
5.7 In this regard, the Committee recommends that LBSNAA institutionalize 
regular, case-based teaching drawn from the Constitution of India, the Constituent 
Assembly Debates and important Parliamentary and Legislative debates to deepen 

 
62 
officers’ appreciation of constitutional values and the role of elected representatives. 
The Committee further recommends that political representatives, including Members 
of Parliament, may be invited, to interact with officer trainees as part of the training 
curriculum. In particular, during district and field training, officer trainees should be 
encouraged to formally engage with the local MLA/MP following due protocol, and 
understand their perspectives and developmental priorities. Such measures would 
enrich the training experience, bridge institutional gaps, and bring civil services 
training closer to democratic ground realities. 
B. Institute of Secretariat Training and Management 
5.8 ISTM is mandated to impart training to officers of Central Secretariat Service (CSS), 
Central Secretariat Stenographers Service (CSSS) and officers of other central services 
functioning in the Central Secretariat. CSS officers form the backbone of the Central 
Government Ministries/ Departments as they assist in the discharge of key responsibilities of 
Department such as policy formulation and implementation, effective monitoring and review. 
5.9 The Committee notes that the Institute of Secretariat Training and Management 
(ISTM) has introduced innovative pedagogical approaches such as the Panch Pranali for 
structured course follow-up and a ‘role visualization’ methodology aimed at preparing 
officers for higher responsibilities. During the deliberations, the Committee appreciated these 
initiatives and emphasized the importance of strengthening functional training in drafting, 
note-writing and core secretariat procedures for officers at various levels. 
5.10 The Committee recommends that ISTM consolidate, document and periodically 
assess the impact of innovations such as Panch Pranali and role visualization with 
measurable outcomes. Based on such assessment, these approaches may be 
systematically mainstreamed in relevant foundational and in-service courses to 
strengthen officers’ competency and preparedness for higher responsibilities. 
C.  Indian Institute of Public Administration 
5.11 Indian Institute of Public Administration (IIPA) was set up to build capacity among 
public servants through training and research with knowledge, skills and behaviour required 
for managing the tasks of governance at the Centre and State level. 
5.12 The Committee appreciates that the IIPA has conducted over 4,666 programmes and 
trained more than 1.52 lakh participants across civil services, defence forces, public sector 
undertakings and elected representatives. The Committee further observes that IIPA’s 

 
63 
flagship Advance Professional Programme in Public Administration (APPPA), a ten-month 
programme sponsored by DoPT, along with its research studies and publications in areas such 
as public administration, climate-smart governance and urban governance, constitutes 
significant institutional strengths.  
5.13 However, during the deliberations, the Committee noted that multiple institutions 
under DoPT, including LBSNAA, ISTM, CBC and IIPA, are engaged in training and 
capacity-building activities. The Committee emphasized the need for clearer role delineation 
and specialization so as to avoid duplication and enhance institutional complementarity. 
5.14 The Committee, therefore, recommends that IIPA, in consultation with 
LBSNAA, ISTM and CBC, clearly define and formalize its niche areas of focus, such as 
advanced public policy, professional programmes like APPPA, urban governance, 
climate-smart governance, and applied public administration research, so as to reduce 
unnecessary overlap in training domains, ensuring distinct value addition and greater 
institutional synergy under Mission Karmayogi. 
D.  Capacity Building Commission 
5.15 Constituted on 1 April 2021, by the Government of India, the Capacity Building 
Commission has been mandated to drive standardisation and harmonisation across the Indian 
Civil Services landscape. As the custodian of civil services capacity building reforms, the 
Commission’s role is central to the overall institutional framework of Mission Karmayogi. 
5.16 Established as an independent body with complete executive and financial autonomy, 
the Commission comprises three Members and is supported by an internal Secretariat. The 
Secretariat is headed by an officer in the grade of Joint Secretary to the GoI (designated as 
the Secretary to the Commission). The Members have been appointed from diverse 
backgrounds to ensure adequate representation of multiple perspectives such as those of state 
governments, public sector, private sector, academia etc. 
5.17 The Committee is pleased to see that the Capacity Building Commission (CBC) has 
made significant progress under Mission Karmayogi, including signing MoUs with 29 
States/UTs, on-boarding a large number of officials onto the iGOT platform, initiating 
capacity-building plans for selected Departments, and launching pilot projects for Panchayats 
and Urban Local Bodies. The Commission has also undertaken outreach workshops with 
urban local bodies and initiated AI-enabled tools for preparation of Capacity Building Plans. 
However, during the deliberations, the Committee emphasized that certain large and critical 

 
64 
States, including Uttar Pradesh, as well as parts of the North-Eastern region, require more 
comprehensive and structured coverage. The Committee also observed that while pilot 
initiatives have been undertaken in select cities and Gram Panchayats, a clear roadmap for 
pan-India expansion, particularly covering all States and urban local bodies in a systematic 
manner, needs to be devised. 
5.18 The Committee, therefore recommends that CBC prioritize expansion of 
capacity-building initiatives to all remaining States and Union Territories, with special 
focus on large States such as Uttar Pradesh and the North-Eastern States, which are not 
yet fully covered. The Committee further recommends that pilot initiatives relating to 
Urban Local Bodies and Panchayats be scaled up in a phased but time-bound manner, 
ensuring that capacity-building frameworks are uniformly rolled out across States, 
including smaller municipalities and rural local bodies. CBC may prepare a clear pan-
India roadmap with defined timelines, priority sectors and measurable milestones to 
ensure nationwide coverage and systematic strengthening of grassroots governance 
under Mission Karmayogi. 
5.19 The Committee notes the significant expansion of capacity building initiatives under 
Mission Karmayogi, including onboarding of over 1.5 crore officials on the iGOT platform, 
completions of more than 7 crore courses, accreditation of training institutes, and introduction 
of competency-based frameworks such as the Karmayogi Competency Model. The 
Committee appreciates these quantitative achievements, however, it observes that systematic 
evaluation of the actual impact of these training interventions on workplace performance, 
behavioural transformation, and improvement in public service delivery has not been clearly 
articulated. 
5.20 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Capacity Building Commission 
should undertake a structured impact assessment of major training programmes 
delivered through the iGOT platform vis-à-vis those conducted through physical, in-
person training modes, so as to evaluate their relative effectiveness in improving 
competencies and workplace outcomes. The study should also incorporate measurable 
indicators relating to functional efficiency, behavioural competencies, quality of 
decision-making, citizen satisfaction, and service delivery timelines. The findings of such 
assessments may be analyzed periodically by the Commission to ensure that capacity 
building efforts translate into demonstrable governance outcomes beyond numerical 
enrolments and course completion statistics.

Chapter 6 
INTEGRITY, VIGILANCE, TRANSPARENCY AND SERVICE 
MATTERS 
 
A. Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) 
6.0 The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) is the premier investigating agency of the 
country entrusted with investigating cases of corruption, major economic offences, banking 
and financial frauds, and other serious conventional crimes. The Bureau also undertakes 
investigation of certain specialized and sensitive matters, including terrorist offences and 
cases of national importance. Cases are referred to the CBI by the Central Government, with 
the concurrence of the concerned State Governments where required, as well as by the 
Hon’ble High Courts and the Hon’ble Supreme Court. 
Human Resource Management 
6.1 The Committee notes that against a sanctioned strength of 7,300 posts, the in-position 
strength of CBI is 6,212, leaving a shortfall of 1,088 posts (14.90%). The rank-wise details of 
sanctioned strength, in-position strength and vacancies are placed at Annexure–I. While the 
Committee appreciates that the vacancy position has reduced from 20.57% in 2024 to 14.90% 
in 2025 and is projected to decline further, the Committee believes that a vacancy level of 
nearly fifteen per cent in a premier investigative agency remains a matter of serious concern.  
6.2 As per the information provided by the Department, the major reasons for vacancies 
are: 
i. CBI is not receiving sufficient & suitable nominations of officers from State Police 
which has traditionally been a major source of induction, particularly in the rank of 
Inspector & SPs; 
ii. Some candidates recommended by UPSC and SSC against the direct recruitment 
quota do not ultimately join the organization because of that there always remain 
some vacancies under Direct Recruitment Quota; 
iii. Delay in sending the relevant documents by lending departments after identifying the 
personnel by CBI for deputation; 
iv. Non identifying suitable / skilled personnel by the lending departments which results 
in non-selection of the personnel for induction even after scrutiny; 
v. There are vacancies in promotion quota because of non-availability of eligible 
officers. 

 
66 
6.3 The Committee notes that one of the major reasons for vacancies under the 
Direct Recruitment quota is that certain candidates recommended by UPSC and SSC 
do not ultimately join the organisation, resulting in persistent shortfalls. The Committee 
is of the view that such avoidable vacancies should not be allowed to spill over and affect 
operational efficiency. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a system of 
maintaining a reserve panel/waitlist, in consultation with the recruiting agencies, may 
be institutionalised so that vacancies arising due to this phenomenon can be filled in a 
time-bound manner without initiating a fresh recruitment cycle. 
6.4 The Committee further notes that as informed by the Department, there are 77 
vacancies out of 500 posts in the Sub-Inspector grade as on 31.12.2025. A high attrition rate 
has also been indicated in this cadre. Considering that Sub-Inspector is the feeder grade for 
supervisory positions and forms the backbone of investigation work, the Committee views 
this as a matter of serious concern. While the Committee acknowledges the earlier reforms in 
Recruitment Rules and introduction of the Limited Departmental Competitive Examination 
(LDCE) to improve career progression, it notes that some structural challenges in cadre 
management continue to persist. 
6.5 The Committee recommends that a detailed root cause analysis be undertaken to 
examine the reasons for attrition in the SI cadre, including issues relating to workload, 
career progression, working conditions, transfers, training, and inter-organisational 
mobility. Based on such analysis, appropriate corrective measures may be introduced to 
enhance retention and morale. 
6.6 The Committee emphasizes that sustained and coordinated efforts are necessary to 
reduce vacancies to minimal levels so that the operational efficiency, investigative capacity 
and institutional credibility of the CBI are not compromised. 
 
Centralized Case Management System (CCMS) 
6.7 The Committee is pleased to note that the CCMS has been made functional within the 
Bureau and contains details of all cases being handled by the CBI. Additionally, certain non-
sensitive information such as searches, arrests, filing of charge-sheets and convictions is 
being periodically placed in the public domain through the CBI website. The Committee also 
appreciates that in compliance with the directions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, 
FIRs are being uploaded on the CBI website and FIRs involving searches are uploaded after 
their completion, in order to maintain confidentiality. 

 
67 
6.8 However, the Committee observes that the core issue underlying its earlier 
recommendations made in the 122nd, 126th and 145th Reports, such as, structured and 
systematic public disclosure of consolidated case statistics and publication of the CBI’s 
Annual Report in the public domain, remains unaddressed. While selective updates are 
posted on the website, these do not substitute for comprehensive, periodic statistical 
disclosures that would enable meaningful public understanding of pendency, disposal 
rates, conviction rates and category-wise case status. 
6.9 In a bid to strengthen institutional accountability, the Committee reiterates its 
earlier recommendation that the CBI should place its Annual Report in the public 
domain with appropriate safeguards for classified or sensitive information; and develop 
a comprehensive framework for periodic publication of consolidated and non-sensitive 
case statistics, including data on registration, pendency, disposal and conviction rates. 
Moreover, a clear timeline be indicated for the public interface of the Centralized Case 
Management System. 
CBI Courts 
6.10 During the deliberations, the Committee was apprised of the current practice about the 
posting of senior-level judges in CBI-designated Courts,which results in limited tenures due 
to their superannuation. Such short tenures, particularly at the senior level, may result in 
disruption of judicial continuity, loss of familiarity with voluminous records and technical 
evidence, and consequent delays in trial proceedings, particularly in complex corruption and 
economic offence matters. 
6.11 The Committee is of the view that specialized courts dealing with CBI cases 
require stability and judicial continuity to ensure timely adjudication and effective 
prosecution. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department, in 
consultation with the concerned High Courts, explore the feasibility of ensuring a 
reasonable and fixed tenure for judicial officers posted to CBI-designated Courts. The 
Committee further recommends that junior and mid-level judges may be posted to such 
Courts for an adequate duration so as to ensure continuity and development of domain 
expertise. 
Cybercrime 
6.12 The Committee notes with serious concern the growing menace of cybercrime, 
particularly cases where fraudsters impersonate officers of premier investigative agencies, 

 
68 
including the CBI and intimidate victims through threats of legal action, arrest or financial 
penalties, thereby coercing them to transfer money. The Committee observes that senior 
citizens are especially vulnerable to such tactics due to limited digital literacy, lack of 
familiarity with cyber fraud methods and heightened susceptibility to fear-based 
manipulation. Such impersonation not only causes financial and emotional distress to victims 
but also risks undermining public trust in investigative institutions. 
6.13 The Committee recommends that the CBI, in coordination with the Ministry of 
Home Affairs and State Governments, undertake targeted public awareness campaigns, 
particularly in regional languages and through platforms accessible to senior citizens, 
clarifying that the Bureau does not demand money or conduct investigations through 
unofficial digital channels. The Committee further recommends strengthening rapid-
response mechanisms in coordination with banks and digital payment platforms to 
enable immediate freezing of suspected fraudulent transactions. Moreover, the 
Committee underscores the need for enhancing inter-agency coordination to dismantle 
organized cyber fraud networks impersonating public officials, and continuously 
upgrading the capacity of investigating officers in emerging cybercrime domains, 
including digital forensics and crypto currency-related offences. 
Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) 
6.14 The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) is the apex integrity institution responsible 
for tendering advice on vigilance matters relating to the Central Government and its 
organisations. It exercises jurisdiction over all matters to which the executive power of the 
Union extends. The Commission functions as an independent statutory body. 
Granting Prosecution Sanctions under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 
6.15 The Committee notes that delays continue to be observed in the grant of prosecution 
sanction under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. As informed by the Commission, 
such delays are often attributed to requests for clarifications from investigating agencies or 
administrative authorities before a decision is taken on sanction proposals. While the 
Committee appreciates that periodic review meetings are held by CVC with the CBI and 
guidelines have been issued by DoPT to minimize delays, the issue of timely and accountable 
decision-making in prosecution sanctions remains a matter of concern. 
6.16 The Committee further recalls that in its 145th Report (Para 6.15), it had 
recommended the establishment of a Centralized Digital Case Repository (CDCR) for secure 

 
69 
storage and instant retrieval of case records, along with mandatory timelines and 
accountability mechanisms for administrative authorities. In response, CVC had stated that 
MeitY’s DigiLocker platform may serve as a repository framework and that the 
recommendation would be taken up with MeitY.  
6.17  The Committee notes that there are delays in prosecution sanction and 
recommends that the Commission, in coordination with DoPT and MeitY, provide an 
updated status on the proposed Centralized Digital Case Repository. The Committee 
may be apprised of the present status of consultations with MeitY regarding integration 
with DigiLocker or any alternative digital repository system. Further, the Committee 
desires that a clear timeline be indicated for full operationalization of a digital tracking 
and repository mechanism to ensure expeditious and transparent disposal of 
prosecution sanction cases.

years (2022, 2023 & 2024). The details are given below:

and review functions, furnish consolidated stage-wise data for the last three years 
indicating the average time taken at key stages of vigilance processing, including 
investigation, reference to the Commission, consideration of advice, and issuance of 
final orders, based on information available with it or received from 
Ministries/Departments. The Commission may also indicate the number of cases 
pending beyond the timelines prescribed in the Vigilance Manual at stages that require 
its review or advisory intervention. Such data would enable a clearer understanding of 
systemic delays and trends in vigilance administration. 
6.22 The Committee is pleased to note that the Commission has developed the 
Vigilance Case Management System (VCMS) to monitor receipt, disposal and 
implementation of its advice. The Committee recommends the VCMS may be further 
leveraged to incorporate comprehensive stage-wise tracking of cases from the stage of 
complaint and investigation at the departmental level through inquiry, Commission 
advice and final disposal, with automated flagging of cases pending beyond the timelines 
prescribed in the Vigilance Manual. Periodic analytical reports may be generated from 
the system to identify recurring bottlenecks across Ministries and organizations. Such 
enhanced monitoring would help detect systemic delays early and promote compliance 
with the timelines prescribed in the Vigilance Manual. 
Uniformity in Vigilance Frameworks across Public Sector Entities 
6.23 The Committee takes note of certain challenges faced by the Commission in ensuring 
uniform implementation of vigilance instructions across CPSEs, Public Sector Banks, Public 
Sector Insurance Companies and other autonomous bodies. These include the lack of an 
effective and structured vigilance set-up and non-appointment of Chief Vigilance Officers in 
Joint Ventures, Special Purpose Vehicles and subsidiaries; uneven or absent provisions in 
certain CPSEs for initiating or continuing disciplinary proceedings against retired employees; 
and lack of uniformity in service regulations of PSBs and PSICs, particularly in dealing with 
composite cases. 
6.24 The Committee recommends that the Commission, in consultation with the 
concerned Ministries and regulatory authorities, undertake a structured review of these 
gaps and issue appropriate advisories to promote greater uniformity in vigilance 

 
71 
frameworks across CPSEs, banks, insurance companies and their subsidiaries. 
Particular attention may be given to ensuring structured vigilance set-ups in JVs/SPVs 
and subsidiaries, harmonisation of provisions relating to action against retired 
employees, and standardisation of service regulations dealing with composite cases, so 
as to strengthen consistency and effectiveness in vigilance administration. 
Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) 
6.25 The Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) was established in 1985 to provide 
speedy and cost-effective redressal to government employees aggrieved by decisions relating 
to service matters. The Tribunal adjudicates service-related disputes that were earlier dealt 
with by courts up to and including the High Courts. At present, CAT functions through 19 
regular Benches across the country, including its Principal Bench at Delhi. 
Pendency of Cases Pending for More than Ten Years 
6.26 The Committee acknowledges that the number of cases pending for more than ten 
years has shown a gradual decline, decreasing from 1,394 cases as on 31.12.2023 to 1,321 
cases as on 31.12.2024 and further to 1,238 cases as on 31.12.2025. However, the number of 
such cases remains significant. The Tribunal has informed that the key constraints in disposal 
of such long-pending matters include the following: 
cases adjourned sine-die due to related matters being sub-judice before the Hon’ble 
Supreme Court or High Courts; cases restored or remanded after long intervals while 
retaining their original institution dates; matters initially dismissed in default and 
subsequently restored; and repeated adjournments sought by counsel for filing replies or 
rejoinders. 
6.27 The Committee further notes that while special drives are conducted from time to 
time based on pendency assessment, there is no proposal to institutionalize such drives as a 
regular mechanism. Given the age of these cases, their prolonged pendency undermines 
timely access to justice, particularly in service and pension-related matters. 
6.28 The Committee is conscious of the judicial and procedural constraints that may 
affect the disposal of certain long-pending cases. However, the continued pendency of 
cases for more than ten years remains a matter of serious concern and warrants priority 
attention. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Tribunal adopt a structured 
and periodic review mechanism for such cases, with focused listing and appropriate 
time-bound disposal strategies, to the extent feasible within the existing legal 

 
72 
framework. While special drives may continue as required, the monitoring of cases 
pending for over ten years may be institutionalised through regular review at the level 
of the Chairman to ensure sustained reduction in pendency and to prevent 
accumulation of similarly aged cases in future. 
Status of operationalizing the Advance Case Information System (ACIS) in CAT 
6.29 The Committee notes with appreciation that the work of scanning and 
digitization of judicial records is being carried out in a phased manner across all 
Benches of CAT, and that implementation of the Document Management System (DMS) 
in the Principal Bench was tentatively targeted for July, 2025, with full roll-out across 
all Benches expected by December, 2025. The Committee commends the progress made 
towards operationalizing a paperless and digitally enabled judicial system. In this 
regard, the Committee may be apprised of the current status of completion of 
digitization across Benches, operationalization of DMS (including e-Court/Smart Court 
components), and whether the targeted timelines have been adhered to. The Committee 
would also like to know the impact, if any, of ACIS implementation on case 
management efficiency and disposal rates thus far. 
Central Information Commission 
6.30 The Central Information Commission (CIC) was constituted by the Central 
Government under Section 12 of the Right to Information Act, 2005. The Commission 
comprises one Chief Information Commissioner and ten Information Commissioners, and 
was formally established through a Gazette Notification dated 11 October 2005. The CIC 
exercises the powers and performs the functions assigned to it under the Act to ensure 
effective implementation of the right to information framework. 
Staff Strength and Vacancy

it had appreciated the efforts made by the Commission to fill vacancies in the ASO and SA 
grades through SSC, but had expressed concern regarding the delay in revival of 48 deemed 
abolished posts across key operational cadres. The Committee had emphasized that a stable 
workforce with streamlined recruitment cycles is essential for ensuring administrative 
efficiency and operational effectiveness. 
6.32 The Committee notes from the updated response that, pursuant to requests made by

received for two more posts, while the remaining posts are under consideration with the

also been taken up and reminders have been issued. 
6.33 While appreciating the progress made in securing approval for partial revival of 
deemed abolished posts, the Committee notes that a substantial number of posts across 
critical support and administrative cadres continue to remain vacant. Given that only 
65 out of 144 sanctioned posts are presently in position, leaving 79 vacancies (of which 
47 are deemed abolished and 11 encadred), the Committee reiterates its earlier 
recommendation that the matter be pursued with utmost priority.  
6.34 The Committee recommends that coordinated efforts be intensified with the 
Department of Expenditure and the concerned divisions of DoPT to secure early 
decision on the remaining proposals for revival and to ensure expeditious filling of both 
revived and encadred posts, so that the Commission’s functional capacity is not 
adversely affected. 
AppCoMS and Technological Upgradation 
6.35 The Committee is pleased to note that the Appeal and Complaint Monitoring System 
(AppCoMS) has contributed to improving efficiency in registration, hearing and disposal of 
cases by enabling real-time tracking and streamlined case management. However, certain 
limitations have been identified by CIC, including absence of secure user authentication and 
lack of dedicated modules for early hearing and time-barred cases. These gaps are proposed 
to be addressed through the upgraded AppCoMS 2.0. 
6.36 As a step to plug the existing gaps, the Committee recommends that AppCoMS 
2.0 be implemented in a time-bound manner, incorporating secure authentication 
mechanisms, modules for early hearing and time-barred cases, and enhanced 
compliance monitoring features. The Commission may periodically assess the impact of 
the upgraded system on disposal rates, pendency reduction and transparency to ensure 
that technological interventions translate into measurable efficiency gains. 
Lokpal 
6.37 The Lokpal is a statutory anti-corruption institution established under the Lokpal and 
Lokayuktas Act, 2013 to inquire into allegations of corruption against specified public 

 
74 
functionaries within its jurisdiction. In accordance with Section 3(2) of the Act, the Lokpal 
comprises a Chairperson and up to eight Members, including both judicial and non-judicial 
Members. 
Constitution of the Inquiry Wing, Prosecution Wing and a Special Court 
 
6.38 The Committee recalls its earlier recommendation in its 145th and 159th reports that 
the Inquiry Wing and Prosecution Wing of the Lokpal be fully constituted within six months 
to enable effective discharge of its statutory mandate.  
6.39 With regard to the Inquiry Wing, the Committee notes that under Sections 10 and 11 
of the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013, the Lokpal is required to constitute an Inquiry Wing 
headed by a Director of Inquiry for conducting preliminary inquiries. The Committee further 
notes that the Inquiry Wing has been formally constituted pursuant to resolutions of the Full 
Bench and notified vide Order dated 05.09.2024, and that an approved Organogram has been 
adopted. At the same time, the Committee takes note of the provision under Section 20 of the 
Act, which empowers the Lokpal to entrust inquiries and investigations to agencies such as 
the CVC and the CBI, and that such arrangements are presently being adopted on a case-to-
case basis. 
6.40 The Committee further notes that 70 regular posts have been created with the 
concurrence of the Department of Expenditure and encadred into CSS, CSSS and 
CSCS, with some posts filled under the Central Staffing Scheme. However, it has been 
observed that appointment of the Director of Inquiry and staffing of the Inquiry Wing 
in accordance with the approved Organogram is still under process. The Committee, 
therefore, desires to be apprised of the present status of appointment of the Director of 
Inquiry and the steps taken to operationalize the Inquiry Wing in its full statutory form, 
while ensuring effective coordination with existing investigative agencies. 
6.41 With regard to prosecution, the Committee notes that the Prosecution Wing of 
the Lokpal has been formally constituted vide Order dated 06.06.2025 and notified in 
the Gazette of India on 13.06.2025. The Committee further notes that, at present, 
matters relating to prosecution are being handled through the CBI, which has its own 
prosecution mechanism. While taking note of the constitution of the Prosecution Wing, 
the Committee desires to be apprised of the present stage of operationalization of the 
Prosecution Wing and the proposed roadmap for making it fully functional in 
accordance with the statutory framework.

desires to be apprised of the present status of consultations with the High Court and the

OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS FOR GRANTS (2026-27) OF THE 
DEPARTMENT OF PERSONNEL AND TRAINING (MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, 
PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS) 
1. The Committee notes that during 2023-24 and 2024-25, Revised Estimates 
exceeded Budget Estimates by 13.0% and 10.6% respectively, yet actual 
expenditure fell short of the Revised Estimates by 5.43% and 2.59%. Further, in 
2025-26, actual expenditure up to 31.01.2026 reflects a shortfall of 25.34% vis-à-
vis the Revised Estimates. At the same time, the Budget Estimates approved by 
the Ministry of Finance have ranged between 60.32% and 84.26% of the 
projected outlays over the last five years. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry undertake a comprehensive review of its budget 
formulation and expenditure management processes. The Committee is also of 
the view that greater realism in projections and improved execution discipline 
would enhance fiscal credibility and strengthen the Ministry’s case during pre-
budget consultations.                      (Para 2.9) 
2. The Committee notes that the performance of the three Departments of the 
Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions on the fiscal front needs 
to be improved. While DoPT has utilized only 75% of the funds allocated to it till 
31st January 2026, DARPG and DPPW are lagging far behind. As per the 
guidelines issued by the Ministry of Finance, expenditure in the last quarter of 
the financial year should ordinarily not exceed 33 per cent of the total Budget 
Estimates, and expenditure during the month of March should not exceed 15 per 
cent of the total Budget Estimates. In this context, the Committee emphasizes 
that the Department(s) must ensure that expenditure during the remaining 
months of the financial year is planned and paced in a manner consistent with 
these prescribed norms.                  (Para 2.15) 
3. The Committee notes that the average rate of expenditure across attached and 
subordinate offices stands at approximately 73.45 per cent as on 31 January 
2026. Considering that ten months of the financial year have elapsed, this reflects 
a slower-than-desirable pace of expenditure. The Committee further observes 
considerable variation in utilisation levels across organisations. In particular, the 
Staff Selection Commission (50.45 per cent) and the Institute of Secretariat 

 
79 
Training and Management (56 per cent) have recorded utilisation levels 
significantly below the desirable benchmark, with substantial unspent balances 
remaining.                      (Para 2.18)

Despite receiving an additional funds at the Revised Estimates 2025-26 stage 
(from ₹515.15 crore (BE) to ₹548.50 crore (RE)), only 50.45 per cent of the funds 
have been utilized as on 31 January 2026, leaving an unspent balance of ₹271.79

₹719.13 crore, whereas the approved Budget Estimate stands at ₹525.20 crore

expenditure trends and the ability of the organization to utilize the funds within

should strengthen quarterly expenditure system monitoring and ensure strict 
adherence to the Ministry of Finance guidelines regarding even pacing of 
expenditure. As reflected in Table IX, the average utilization across

stage for 2026-27, organizations such as Lokpal received only 20.24 per cent of

21. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendations made in the 
126th and 145th Reports that the Department finalise its decision on the 
Chandramouli Committee’s recommendations within a clearly defined 
timeframe and communicate the same to the Committee. At the policy level, the 
Committee recommends that annual intake planning of Direct Recruit IAS 
officers should follow a data-driven mechanism, and the projected intake should 

 
84 
be aligned with cadre-wise projected retirement data, anticipated attrition and 
administrative requirements.                 (Para 3.11) 
22. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department examine the 
feasibility of institutionalising a structured 360-degree review mechanism, for 
empanelment of Joint Secretary and other higher posts drawn from services 
other than the IAS. Such an approach would promote parity in evaluation 
standards across services, strengthen merit-based selection at senior levels, and 
enhance confidence in the objectivity and robustness of the empanelment 
process.                        (Para 3.15) 
23. The Committee is of the view that personnel management must extend beyond 
recruitment and cadre strength to encompass the holistic well-being and 
sustainability of the administrative workforce. The Committee recommends that 
the Department of Personnel & Training, in consultation with cadre controlling 
authorities and State Governments, develop a structured framework for officer 
well-being, including institutionalized mental health/counseling support 
mechanisms, periodic monitoring of prolonged additional charge assignments, 
reasonable tenure stability as against frequent transfers, integration of stress-
management modules under Mission Karmayogi, and consider annual well-being 
surveys to identify systemic stress factors. The Committee believes that proactive 
attention to officer well-being will enhance administrative effectiveness, reduce 
burnout risks and contribute to better governance outcomes.             (Para 3.17) 
24. The Committee recommends that the Department, in coordination with relevant 
Ministries and Departments, take the lead in developing a comprehensive 
Government-wide framework for the ethical, secure and accountable use of 
Artificial Intelligence in public administration. Such a framework should clearly 
define safeguards for data protection and confidentiality, ensure proper record-
keeping of AI-assisted actions, and retain final decision-making authority with 
designated human officers. This is particularly important as AI tools across 
Ministries may handle varied and sensitive categories of data, including 
personnel, financial, regulatory and citizen-related information.          (Para 3.20) 
25. The Committee further recommends that the use of AI tools for official purposes 
be governed through centrally approved enterprise-level agreements with service 
providers, including Large Language Model (LLM) platforms, so as to ensure 

 
85 
confidentiality of Government data, compliance with national data protection 
and security standards, and clear contractual safeguards regarding data storage, 
processing and access.                             (Para 3.21) 
26. The Committee further recommends that AI-enabled systems adopted by 
Ministries adhere to robust information security protocols and confidentiality 
safeguards, particularly in handling service records, vigilance matters, 
performance data, financial transactions and other sensitive government 
information.                         (Para 3.22) 
27. The Committee also emphasizes the need to expand AI literacy and responsible-
use training across all levels of government, particularly for dealing hands and 
lower-level staff who routinely process official data, so that technological 
adoption is accompanied by awareness of ethical boundaries, confidentiality 
obligations and cyber-security safeguards.               (Para 3.23) 
RECRUITMENT INSTITUTIONS 
28. The Committee welcomes this development as a step towards enhancing 
transparency, fairness and candidate confidence in the examination process. 
However, the Committee desires to be apprised of the detailed modalities framed 
by the Commission, pertaining to the timeline for publication of the provisional 
answer key after the Preliminary Examination; the mechanism and time window 
for submission of objections by candidates; and the process for examination and 
disposal of such objections. The Committee may also be informed whether the 
final answer key along with a reasoned clarification on accepted/rejected 
objections will also be placed in the public domain.     (Para 4.4) 
29. The Committee recognizes the importance of assessing analytical ability, 
comprehension and decision-making skills in prospective civil servants. At the 
same time, the Committee is of the view that the Preliminary Examination 
should ensure a level-playing field for candidates from varied academic streams. 
Although the CSAT paper is qualifying in nature, the Committee recommends 
that the Union Public Service Commission undertake a comprehensive review to 
rationalize the CSAT component, including its syllabus and level of difficulty, so 
as to assess its impact across different academic backgrounds.  The review may 
be supported by empirical analysis of candidate performance patterns to ensure 

 
86 
that the examination continues to uphold principles of fairness, inclusivity and 
equal opportunity. 
(Para 4.6) 
30. The Committee considers any that misuse of PwBD or EWS certificates in 
recruitment is a matter of serious concern, as it undermines the principles of 
equity, transparency and fairness that underpin public employment. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Personnel and 
Training, in consultation with UPSC and other recruiting agencies, strengthen 
verification mechanisms for PwBD and EWS certificates at appropriate stages of 
the recruitment process. The Committee further recommends that technology-
enabled verification systems, including advanced digital scrutiny tools where 
feasible, be explored to detect forged or manipulated certificates in a timely 
manner. Such measures may include digital validation, systematic cross-
verification with issuing authorities, and close coordination with the State 
Governments and competent certification bodies.     (Para 4.8) 
31. The Committee notes the position explained by the Commission. While 
recognising the constitutional requirement of laying the Reports before 
Parliament, the Committee emphasises that timely finalisation and presentation 
of Annual Reports is essential for ensuring transparency and accountability. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Commission adhere to a definite 
timeline for preparation and laying of its Annual Reports and avoid undue 
delays in future.                        (Para 4.10) 
32. The Committee notes that the matter remains under examination and that no 
specific timeline has yet been indicated for implementation of the reforms. While 
recognizing that the recommendations have broad policy implications, the 
Committee opines that prolonged consideration without indicative timelines may 
delay necessary reforms in a critical national recruitment process. The 
Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation that a structured 
and phased implementation roadmap be prepared, identifying reforms that may 
be taken up in the short term and those requiring wider consultation, and that 
the Committee be apprised of the progress made in this regard.           (Para 4.14) 
33. The Committee is pleased to note that 292 organizations have registered on the 
PRATIBHA SETU Portal. However, it also observes that employers are not 
regularly updating the status of selected candidates on the portal. While 

 
87 
welcoming the outreach efforts undertaken by UPSC, the Committee 
recommends that a structured monitoring mechanism be put in place to ensure 
regular updating by registered organizations and to assess the actual placement 
outcomes under the Scheme. The Committee further recommends that periodic 
feedback be obtained from participating organizations as well as candidates to 
evaluate the effectiveness and impact of the initiative. An annual performance 
review of the Portal, including data on registrations, placements and feedback 
received, may also be incorporated in the Commission’s Annual Report.  
(Para 4.16) 
34. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Staff Selection Commission 
expeditiously finalize and implement a structured sliding mechanism /counseling 
system with clearly defined timelines so that reported vacancies are optimally 
utilized within the same recruitment cycle. Moreover, the Committee 
recommends that SSC examine the feasibility of maintaining a reserve/waiting 
list on the lines of the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC), so that 
vacancies arising due to non-joining or withdrawal can be promptly filled 
without waiting for the next examination cycle.               (Para 4.19) 
35. The Committee feels that SSC being a premier national recruiting agency, must 
ensure that its recruitment processes do not, even inadvertently, lead to regional 
concentration in recruitment outcomes. The Commission must conduct an 
analytical study to examine whether structural factors, such as awareness levels, 
access to coaching, digital infrastructure, language barriers, or examination 
centre distribution, are contributing to regional disparities. The Committee 
further recommends to formulate a targeted outreach strategy for 
underrepresented regions, particularly the North-East, tribal districts, rural 
areas and Aspirational Districts, including awareness campaigns in local 
languages, and increasing presence of examination centres in remote areas.  
(Para 4.21) 
36. The Committee, therefore, recommends that NRA adhere to the proposed three-
month timeline and furnish a clear implementation schedule indicating key 
milestones. Once SSC, RRBs and IBPS are on boarded, other Central Public 
Examination Authorities should be brought onto the UOTR platform in a time-
bound and phased manner to ensure uniform adoption. The Committee also 

 
88 
emphasizes that robust data security and audit safeguards must be ensured prior 
to full-scale rollout.                   (Para 4.25) 
37. The Committee, therefore, recommends that NRA finalize and notify uniform 
CBT standards and technical protocols within a defined timeframe. Moreover, 
prior to nationwide rollout, NRA should undertake a comprehensive capacity 
assessment of examination infrastructure and adopt a phased implementation 
strategy based on logistical readiness. The Committee further recommends that 
a preparedness assessment be conducted before commencement of the first full-
scale CET cycle.                 (Para 4.28) 
38. The Committee opines that the concerned Department must examine the 
adequacy of sanctioned and functional manpower in NRA in view of its 
expanding mandate. Key leadership positions should be filled on a full-time basis 
to ensure institutional stability and accountability. A realistic manpower 
augmentation plan be prepared before full-scale rollout of CET and UOTR is 
achieved.                         (Para 4.30) 
39. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that PESB should set timelines for 
each stage of the selection process, including vigilance clearance and scheduling 
of meetings. In terms of the foreseen vacancies, the pre-advertisement processes, 
particularly timely submission and finalization of job descriptions, can be 
streamlined in coordination with Administrative Ministries. Advance action for 
foreseen vacancies will ensure that candidate recommendations are made well 
before vacancy occurrence, thereby making the process efficient.         (Para 4.34) 
40. The Committee recommends that PESB maintain a comprehensive vacancy 
tracking dashboard reflecting existing, anticipated and pipeline vacancies, to be 
periodically reviewed in consultation with Administrative Ministries. The 
Committee further recommends that in cases where selection meetings conclude 
without recommendation, the reasons thereof, including inadequacy of applicant 
pool, restrictive eligibility conditions, or non-availability of suitable candidates, 
be systematically analyzed. Moreover, such posts should be re-advertised within 
a defined timeframe to prevent prolonged vacancies and ensure continuity of 
leadership in CPSEs.                  (Para 4.38) 
  

 
89 
TRAINING INSTITUTIONS 
41. The Committee, therefore, recommends that all vacant faculty posts, particularly 
in areas such as Law, Management, Economics, Social Management, and Hindi 
& Regional Languages, be filled in a time-bound manner to ensure academic 
depth, continuity and training quality. The Committee further recommends that 
the Academy undertake a structured cadre review to assess whether the existing 
sanctioned strength adequately reflects its expanding mandate under Mission 
Karmayogi, especially in emerging domains such as digital governance, artificial 
intelligence, climate policy, and public finance which may require domain 
experts.                     (Para 5.3) 
42. To strengthen the service ethos amongst civil servants, the Committee 
recommends that LBSNAA should systematically integrate modules on 
seva‑bhav and ‘frequency matching’ with citizens, into the Foundation Course, 
district training and mid‑career programmes, with specific practical exercises on 
dealing empathetically with common people, especially the poor, elderly, farmers 
and vulnerable groups.        (Para 5.5) 
43. In this regard, the Committee recommends that LBSNAA institutionalize 
regular, case-based teaching drawn from the Constitution of India, the 
Constituent Assembly Debates and important Parliamentary and Legislative 
debates to deepen officers’ appreciation of constitutional values and the role of 
elected representatives. The Committee further recommends that political 
representatives, including Members of Parliament, may be invited, to interact 
with officer trainees as part of the training curriculum. In particular, during 
district and field training, officer trainees should be encouraged to formally 
engage with the local MLA/MP following due protocol, and understand their 
perspectives and developmental priorities. Such measures would enrich the 
training experience, bridge institutional gaps, and bring civil services training 
closer to democratic ground realities.              (Para 5.7) 
44. The Committee recommends that ISTM consolidate, document and periodically 
assess the impact of innovations such as Panch Pranali and role visualization 
with measurable outcomes. Based on such assessment, these approaches may be 
systematically mainstreamed in relevant foundational and in-service courses to 
strengthen officers’ competency and preparedness for higher responsibilities.  
(Para 5.10) 

 
90 
45. The Committee, therefore, recommends that IIPA, in consultation with 
LBSNAA, ISTM and CBC, clearly define and formalize its niche areas of focus, 
such as advanced public policy, professional programmes like APPPA, urban 
governance, climate-smart governance, and applied public administration 
research, so as to reduce unnecessary overlap in training domains, ensuring 
distinct value addition and greater institutional synergy under Mission 
Karmayogi.                         (Para 5.14) 
46. The Committee, therefore recommends that CBC prioritize expansion of 
capacity-building initiatives to all remaining States and Union Territories, with 
special focus on large States such as Uttar Pradesh and the North-Eastern States, 
which are not yet fully covered. The Committee further recommends that pilot 
initiatives relating to Urban Local Bodies and Panchayats be scaled up in a 
phased but time-bound manner, ensuring that capacity-building frameworks are 
uniformly rolled out across States, including smaller municipalities and rural 
local bodies. CBC may prepare a clear pan-India roadmap with defined 
timelines, priority sectors and measurable milestones to ensure nationwide 
coverage and systematic strengthening of grassroots governance under Mission 
Karmayogi.                         (Para 5.18) 
47. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Capacity Building Commission 
should undertake a structured impact assessment of major training programmes 
delivered through the iGOT platform vis-à-vis those conducted through physical, 
in-person training modes, so as to evaluate their relative effectiveness in 
improving competencies and workplace outcomes. The study should also 
incorporate measurable indicators relating to functional efficiency, behavioural 
competencies, quality of decision-making, citizen satisfaction, and service 
delivery timelines. The findings of such assessments may be analyzed 
periodically by the Commission to ensure that capacity building efforts translate 
into demonstrable governance outcomes beyond numerical enrolments and 
course completion statistics.                 (Para 5.20)  
INTEGRITY, VIGILANCE, TRANSPARENCY AND SERVICE MATTERS 
48. The Committee notes that one of the major reasons for vacancies under the 
Direct Recruitment quota is that certain candidates recommended by UPSC and 
SSC do not ultimately join the organisation, resulting in persistent shortfalls. 
The Committee is of the view that such avoidable vacancies should not be 

 
91 
allowed to spill over and affect operational efficiency. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that a system of maintaining a reserve panel/waitlist, in 
consultation with the recruiting agencies, may be institutionalised so that 
vacancies arising due to this phenomenon can be filled in a time-bound manner 
without initiating a fresh recruitment cycle.       (Para 6.3) 
49. The Committee recommends that a detailed root cause analysis be undertaken to 
examine the reasons for attrition in the SI cadre, including issues relating to 
workload, career progression, working conditions, transfers, training, and inter-
organisational mobility. Based on such analysis, appropriate corrective measures 
may be introduced to enhance retention and morale.     (Para 6.5) 
50. However, the Committee observes that the core issue underlying its earlier 
recommendations made in the 122nd, 126th and 145th Reports, such as, 
structured and systematic public disclosure of consolidated case statistics and 
publication of the CBI’s Annual Report in the public domain, remains 
unaddressed. While selective updates are posted on the website, these do not 
substitute for comprehensive, periodic statistical disclosures that would enable 
meaningful public understanding of pendency, disposal rates, conviction rates 
and category-wise case status.         (Para 6.8) 
51. In a bid to strengthen institutional accountability, the Committee reiterates its 
earlier recommendation that the CBI should place its Annual Report in the 
public domain with appropriate safeguards for classified or sensitive 
information; and develop a comprehensive framework for periodic publication 
of consolidated and non-sensitive case statistics, including data on registration, 
pendency, disposal and conviction rates. Moreover, a clear timeline be indicated 
for the public interface of the Centralized Case Management System.   (Para 6.9) 
52. The Committee is of the view that specialized courts dealing with CBI cases 
require stability and judicial continuity to ensure timely adjudication and 
effective prosecution. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Department, in consultation with concerned High Courts, explore the feasibility 
of ensuring a reasonable and fixed tenure for judicial officers posted to CBI-
designated Courts. The Committee further recommends that junior and mid-
level judges may be posted to such Courts for an adequate duration so as to 
ensure continuity and development of domain expertise.                      (Para 6.11) 

 
92 
53. The Committee recommends that the CBI, in coordination with the Ministry of 
Home Affairs and State Governments, undertake targeted public awareness 
campaigns, particularly in regional languages and through platforms accessible 
to senior citizens, clarifying that the Bureau does not demand money or conduct 
investigations through unofficial digital channels. The Committee further 
recommends strengthening rapid-response mechanisms in coordination with 
banks and digital payment platforms to enable immediate freezing of suspected 
fraudulent transactions. Moreover, the Committee underscores the need for 
enhancing inter-agency coordination to dismantle organized cyber fraud 
networks impersonating public officials, and continuously upgrading the 
capacity of investigating officers in emerging cybercrime domains, including 
digital forensics and crypto currency-related offences.              (Para 6.13) 
54. The Committee notes that there are delays in prosecution sanction and 
recommends that the Commission, in coordination with DoPT and MeitY, 
provide an updated status on the proposed Centralized Digital Case Repository. 
The Committee may be apprised of the present status of consultations with 
MeitY regarding integration with DigiLocker or any alternative digital 
repository system. Further, the Committee desires that a clear timeline be 
indicated for full operationalization of a digital tracking and repository 
mechanism to ensure expeditious and transparent disposal of prosecution 
sanction cases.                        (Para 6.17) 
55. The Committee recommends that the Commission, in exercise of its supervisory 
and review functions, furnish consolidated stage-wise data for the last three 
years indicating the average time taken at key stages of vigilance processing, 
including investigation, reference to the Commission, consideration of advice, 
and issuance of final orders, based on information available with it or received 
from Ministries/Departments. The Commission may also indicate the number of 
cases pending beyond the timelines prescribed in the Vigilance Manual at stages 
that require its review or advisory intervention. Such data would enable a 
clearer understanding of systemic delays and trends in vigilance administration. 
(Para 6.21) 
56. The Committee is pleased to note that the Commission has developed the 
Vigilance Case Management System (VCMS) to monitor receipt, disposal and 
implementation of its advice. The Committee recommends the VCMS may be 

 
93 
further leveraged to incorporate comprehensive stage-wise tracking of cases 
from the stage of complaint and investigation at the departmental level through 
inquiry, Commission advice and final disposal, with automated flagging of cases 
pending beyond the timelines prescribed in the Vigilance Manual. Periodic 
analytical reports may be generated from the system to identify recurring 
bottlenecks across Ministries and organizations. Such enhanced monitoring 
would help detect systemic delays early and promote compliance with the 
timelines prescribed in the Vigilance Manual.              (Para 6.22) 
57. The Committee recommends that the Commission, in consultation with the 
concerned Ministries and regulatory authorities, undertake a structured review 
of these gaps and issue appropriate advisories to promote greater uniformity in 
vigilance frameworks across CPSEs, banks, insurance companies and their 
subsidiaries. Particular attention may be given to ensuring structured vigilance 
set-ups in JVs/SPVs and subsidiaries, harmonisation of provisions relating to 
action against retired employees, and standardisation of service regulations 
dealing with composite cases, so as to strengthen consistency and effectiveness in 
vigilance administration.                  (Para 6.24) 
58. The Committee is conscious of the judicial and procedural constraints that may 
affect the disposal of certain long-pending cases. However, the continued 
pendency of cases for more than ten years remains a matter of serious concern 
and warrants priority attention. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Tribunal adopt a structured and periodic review mechanism for such cases, with 
focused listing and appropriate time-bound disposal strategies, to the extent 
feasible within the existing legal framework. While special drives may continue 
as required, the monitoring of cases pending for over ten years may be 
institutionalised through regular review at the level of the Chairman to ensure 
sustained reduction in pendency and to prevent accumulation of similarly aged 
cases in future.                        (Para 6.28) 
59. The Committee notes with appreciation that the work of scanning and 
digitization of judicial records is being carried out in a phased manner across all 
Benches of CAT, and that implementation of the Document Management System 
(DMS) in the Principal Bench was tentatively targeted for July, 2025, with full 
roll-out across all Benches expected by December, 2025. The Committee 
commends the progress made towards operationalizing a paperless and digitally 

 
94 
enabled judicial system. In this regard, the Committee may be apprised of the 
current status of completion of digitization across Benches, operationalization of 
DMS (including e-Court/Smart Court components), and whether the targeted 
timelines have been adhered to. The Committee would also like to know the 
impact, if any, of ACIS implementation on case management efficiency and 
disposal rates thus far.                       (Para 6.29) 
60. While appreciating the progress made in securing approval for partial revival of 
deemed abolished posts, the Committee notes that a substantial number of posts 
across critical support and administrative cadres continue to remain vacant. 
Given that only 65 out of 144 sanctioned posts are presently in position, leaving 
79 vacancies (of which 47 are deemed abolished and 11 encadred), the 
Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation that the matter be pursued 
with utmost priority.                   (Para 6.33) 
61. The Committee recommends that coordinated efforts be intensified with the 
Department of Expenditure and the concerned divisions of DoPT to secure early 
decision on the remaining proposals for revival and to ensure expeditious filling 
of both revived and encadred posts, so that the Commission’s functional capacity 
is not adversely affected.                  (Para 6.34) 
62. As a step to plug the existing gaps, the Committee recommends that AppCoMS 
2.0 be implemented in a time-bound manner, incorporating secure 
authentication mechanisms, modules for early hearing and time-barred cases, 
and enhanced compliance monitoring features. The Commission may 
periodically assess the impact of the upgraded system on disposal rates, 
pendency reduction and transparency to ensure that technological interventions 
translate into measurable efficiency gains.               (Para 6.36) 
63. The Committee further notes that 70 regular posts have been created with the 
concurrence of the Department of Expenditure and encadred into CSS, CSSS 
and CSCS, with some posts filled under the Central Staffing Scheme. However, it 
has been observed that appointment of the Director of Inquiry and staffing of the 
Inquiry Wing in accordance with the approved Organogram is still under 
process. The Committee, therefore, desires to be apprised of the present status of 
appointment of the Director of Inquiry and the steps taken to operationalize the 

 
95 
Inquiry Wing in its full statutory form, while ensuring effective coordination 
with existing investigative agencies.                (Para 6.40) 
64. With regard to prosecution, the Committee notes that the Prosecution Wing of 
the Lokpal has been formally constituted vide Order dated 06.06.2025 and 
notified in the Gazette of India on 13.06.2025. The Committee further notes that, 
at present, matters relating to prosecution are being handled through the CBI, 
which has its own prosecution mechanism. While taking note of the constitution 
of the Prosecution Wing, the Committee desires to be apprised of the present 
stage of operationalization of the Prosecution Wing and the proposed roadmap 
for making it fully functional in accordance with the statutory framework.  
(Para 6.41) 
65. As regards notification of a Special Court under Section 35 of the Lokpal and 
Lokayuktas Act, 2013, the Committee notes that the matter has been taken up 
with the High Court of Delhi and is being actively pursued. The Committee 
further notes that, presently, cases are being tried by Special Judges notified 
under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 pursuant to sanction granted by 
the Lokpal. The Committee desires to be apprised of the present status of 
consultations with the High Court and the expected timeline for notification of a 
dedicated Special Court under Section 35 of the Act.              (Para 6.42) 
66. The Committee recommends that the staffing position of the Lokpal Secretariat 
be reviewed in light of the rising trend in complaints and inquiry activity. 
Vacancies in key operational and support divisions may be filled expeditiously, 
and necessary coordination with the concerned authorities may be undertaken to 
ensure that adequate manpower is made available to enable the Lokpal to 
discharge its statutory functions efficiently and without interruption.  (Para 6.48)

2. At the outset, the Chairman welcomed all Members and apprised them of the agenda 
of the meeting, i.e. to examine the Demands for Grants (2026-27) of DoPT and organizations 
under its administrative control. He then welcomed Ms. Rachna Shah, Secretary, DoPT and 
other officers to the meeting of the Committee and stated  that the Committee wished to be 
apprised of budgetary provisions in 2025-26, utilization of funds, achievements, problem 
areas and constraints including logistics and manpower shortages. The Chairman also 
informed that the Committee also desired to know Department-wise and organization-wise 
thrust areas for the financial year 2026-27.  
3. The Secretary, Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), thanked the Committee 
for the opportunity and made a brief introductory statement. She informed that the 
Department is responsible for personnel policy of the Government, including recruitment, 
examinations, promotions, deputations, vigilance matters and capacity building of 
Government employees. She also highlighted that DoPT manages the cadres of the All India 
Services, serves as the cadre controlling authority for the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) 
and the Central Secretariat Service (CSS), and is responsible for major capacity-building 
initiatives such as Mission Karmayogi.  
4. Shri Rupinder Singh, Additional Secretary & Financial Advisor (AS&FA) made a 
presentation outlining the activities and financial position of the Department as well as the 
vision and key functions, which broadly covered recruitment and reservation policies, 
training and capacity building, service conditions and manpower planning, welfare measures, 
and vigilance and disciplinary matters. He emphasized the Department’s focus on 
strengthening human resource management in Government through transparent, efficient and 
accountable systems. 
5. The AS&FA further apprised the Committee of the overall budgetary position of the 
Department and its organizations. He informed that the Budget Estimates for the current 
financial year were about ₹2,454 crore, which were revised to about ₹2,365 crore at the 
Revised Estimates stage, with expenditure so far being around 75 per cent. Further, he 
mentioned that for the next financial year, a budget outlay of about ₹2,425 crore had been 

 
100 
approved. He also stated that the Department was focusing on data-driven improvements in 
recruitment and personnel management while aligning expenditure with the priorities of 
Mission Karmayogi and broader personnel reforms. 
6.       Thereafter, the AS&FA briefly referred to the Budgetary support for other 
organizations under DoPT's administrative control where funds had been provided to support 
their core functions in the areas of recruitment, training, vigilance, service conditions and 
welfare of Government employees. He underlined that the Department was endeavouring to 
optimize resource-use and to align spending with the priorities of Mission Karmayogi and 
personnel reforms.    
7.      After the presentations, Hon. Members of the Committee raised queries and sought 
clarifications on the adequacy and utilization of Budget allocations, status of key projects and 
reforms in recruitment processes. They also raised questions on functioning and infrastructure 
needs of organizations under DoPT, implementation of Mission Karmayogi, cadre

R E P O R T 
CHAPTER – I 
OVERVIEW OF THE DEPARTMENTS 
MINISTRY 
1.0 The Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions is the coordinating agency 
of the Central Government in personnel matters especially for issues concerning recruitment, 
training, career development, staff welfare as well as to the post retirement dispensation.  
1.1 The Ministry comprises the following three Departments: 
(i) Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT); 
(ii) Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (DARPG); and 
(iii) Department of Pension and Pensioners' Welfare (DoPPW). 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
1.2 The Ministry is presently under the overall charge of the Hon‘ble Prime Minister 
assisted by the Minister of State. The Department of Personnel and Training is functioning 
under the charge of an independent Secretary while the Department of Administrative 
Reforms & Public Grievances and the Department of Pension and Pensioners‘ Welfare are 
functioning under the charge of another Secretary. This report pertains to the Department of 
Administrative Reforms & Public Grievances; and the Department of Pension and 
Pensioners‘ Welfare. 
 
 
 
 


 
2 
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND  
PUBLIC GRIEVANCES (DARPG) 
 
Evolution of the Department 
1.3 In March, 1954, an Organisation and Method (O & M) Division was set up in Cabinet 
Secretariat as a follow up to one of the recommendations made by Paul H. Appleby. In 
March, 1964, a Department of Administrative Reforms was set up within the Ministry of 
Home Affairs and Organisation and Method (O & M) Division was transferred to its charge 
from the Cabinet Secretariat. On 7th February, 1973, the work relating to the Department of 
Administrative Reforms was transferred to Department of Personnel created under Cabinet 
Secretariat on 1st August, 1970 and was re-designated as Department of Personnel and 
Administrative Reforms. In April, 1977, the Department of Personnel and Administrative 
Reforms was shifted from Cabinet Secretariat to the Ministry of Home Affairs. In March 
1985, the Department of Personnel and Administrative Reforms was elevated to a full fledged 
Ministry of Personnel and Training, Administrative Reforms, Public Grievances and 
Pensions. On 10th December, 1985 Ministry of Personnel and Training, Administrative 
Reforms, Public Grievances and Pensions was re-designated as the Ministry of Personnel, 
Public Grievances and Pensions with three Departments namely, Department of Personnel 
and Training (DOPT), Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances and 
Department of Pension and Pensioners Welfare. 
About the Department 
1.4 The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances is the nodal 
agency of the Government of India for administrative reforms as well as for redressal of 
public grievances relating to the States in general and grievances pertaining to Central 
Government agencies in particular. The Department disseminates information on important 
activities of the Government relating to administrative reforms and public grievance redressal 
through publications and documentation. The Department also undertakes activities in the 
field of international exchange and cooperation to promote public service reforms. There are 
8 Divisions in the Department namely Administrative Reforms, Organization & Methods, e-
Governance, Documentation & Dissemination, International Exchange & Cooperation, 
Administration & Coordination, Public Grievances and Administrative Reforms Commission 
(ARC)/e-Office. The Department comes under the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances 
and Pensions and is headed by a Secretary. 
Functions of the Department 
1.5 As per the Government of India Allocation of Business Rules, the following subjects 
have been allocated to the Department of Administrative Reforms & Public Grievances: 
(i) Administrative Reforms, including e-governance and dissemination of best 
  practices. 
(ii) Organization and Methods. 
(iii) Policy, coordination and monitoring of issues relating to: 
(a)  Redress of public grievances in general; and 
(b)  Grievances pertaining to Central Government agencies. 

 
3 
(c) Monitoring of implementation of e-Office in Central Ministries /   
  Departments. 
(iv) (a)  Research in public management; 
       (b)  Liaison with State Governments, professional institutions etc. in public 
   management matters. 
(v) Administration of Central Secretariat Manual of Office Procedure.  
 
1.6 Accordingly, the functions of the Department are as under:  
i. Matters relating to administrative reforms. 
ii. Organization of Civil Services Day and Prime Minister‘s Award for 
Excellence in Public Administration. 
iii. Capacity building, change management, and Government Process Re-
engineering to provide reform through e-governance.

NATIONAL CENTRE FOR GOOD GOVERNANCE (NCGG) 
1.8 National Centre for Good Governance was established as an autonomous institute 
under the aegis of the Department of Personnel and Training by upgrading the erstwhile 
National Institution of Administrative Research, Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of 
Administration, Mussoorie. DARPG has been made the Administrative authority for NCGG 
since 08.11.2017. 
  
1.9 The Centre is envisaged to be the apex think-tank that would guide the Government 
and help in implementing good Governance reforms. It seeks to be a high-level institute for 
research and capacity building to deal with the entire gamut of governance issues from the 
National to State to the local level and in sectors across the Government. 
 
1.10 NCGG is governed by a Governing Body, under the Chairmanship of the Cabinet 
Secretary, GoI and a Management Committee with the Secretary of the Department as the 
Chairperson.  
Objectives of NCGG 
1.11 Following are the objectives of the NCGG:  
 To be a think tank for governance & policy reforms, cutting across 
administrative, social, economic and financial spheres. 
 To function as a national repository on information on best practices, initiatives 
and methodologies that promote Good Governance, E-Governance, innovation 
& change management within the government; 
 To initiate and participate in action research and capacity building on various 
aspects of regulatory and development administration, public policy, governance 
and public management at National/State & local levels; 
 To advise on key issues in governance and development synergy across various 
Ministries/ Departments of GoI, and State Governments; 
 To promote sharing and replication of innovative ideas and best practices in 
Governance.  
 To interact with national and international organizations, in and outside 
government, engaged in research and capacity building in the above spheres.  
 
Mandate of NCGG 
1.12 The mandate of the NCGG is to promote Good Governance by:  
 Carrying out Action Research/ Studies on issues relating to governance. 
 Capacity Building on Public Policy and Governance at both National and 
International level. 
 Organizing consultations, workshops, seminars/webinars & talks to promote 
improved governance. 
 Undertaking initiatives for citizen centric governance.
